articles.title: Autologous stem cell transplantation for multiple myeloma: Experience from a tertiary centre in South India

abstract.heading: Background
abstract.text: Autologous haematopoietic stem cell transplantation (auto-HSCT) remains the standard of care for transplant-eligible patients with newly diagnosed multiple myeloma (NDMM). Real-world single-centre data from India are limited. We report the outcomes of our auto-HSCT program in multiple myeloma (MM), including engraftment kinetics, toxicity profile, and response evolution.

abstract.heading: Methods
abstract.text: We retrospectively analysed 16 consecutive patients with MM who underwent auto-HSCT at KIMSHEALTH between July 2023 and January 2026. Data regarding disease characteristics, induction regimens, mobilisation, conditioning, engraftment, toxicity, and response outcomes were collected.

abstract.heading: Results
abstract.text: The median age at transplantation was 55 years, and the cohort comprised 10 males and six females. Revised International Staging System (R-ISS) distribution was stage I in 31.3%, stage II in 50%, and stage III in 18.7%. VRd-based induction was the most commonly used regimen (56.2%), while 25% received daratumumab as frontline therapy. Plerixafor was used universally (100%). The median CD34+ yield was 7.80 × 10^6^/kg. Median neutrophil and platelet engraftment occurred at D+11 and D+14 respectively. Febrile neutropenia was universal (100%). At D+90, 73.3% achieved stringent complete response (sCR) and 86.7% achieved a very good partial response (≥VGPR). Three patients (18.75%) died from infection or progressive disease; no early transplant-related mortality (TRM) was observed. Two patients had disease relapse.

abstract.heading: Conclusion
abstract.text: KIMSHEALTH's auto-HSCT programme for MM demonstrates excellent stem cell mobilisation, rapid engraftment, and deep response rates comparable to global benchmarks, supporting continued expansion and protocol standardisation.

articles.bodyHtml:
Introduction

Multiple myeloma (MM) is a clonal plasma cell malignancy that accounts for approximately 10% of all haematological malignancies and 1-2% of all cancers. It is characterised by the uncontrolled proliferation of malignant plasma cells within the bone marrow, production of monoclonal immunoglobulin (M-protein), and resultant end-organ damage manifesting as hypercalcaemia, renal failure, anemia, and bone disease, collectively referred to as the CRAB criteria.1

The global incidence of MM is approximately 176,000 new cases per year, with an age-standardised incidence rate of 2.1 per 100,000. In India, while precise epidemiological data are limited, the incidence appears to be increasing, owing to improved diagnostic capabilities and an ageing population.2 MM remains incurable with conventional therapy alone, but outcomes have improved dramatically over the past two decades with the introduction of novel therapeutic agents including immunomodulatory drugs (IMiDs), proteasome inhibitors (PIs), and more recently, daratumumab (anti-CD38 monoclonal antibody), carfilzomib, and bispecific T-cell engagers.

For transplant-eligible patients - generally those younger than 65-70 years with adequate organ function and performance status - high-dose chemotherapy followed by autologous haematopoietic stem cell transplantation (auto-HSCT) with melphalan conditioning remains the backbone of frontline treatment.3 Auto-HSCT has consistently demonstrated superior progression-free survival (PFS) and overall survival (OS) compared to conventional chemotherapy alone, with landmark trials such as IFM 2009 and EMN02/HO95 confirming its benefit even in the era of daratumumab-based induction.4,5

Despite these advances, real-world data from tertiary centres in India, and particularly from Kerala, remain sparse. Challenges unique to the Indian transplant setting include delayed presentation with advanced R-ISS staging, financial constraints, limited access to novel agents, and a high burden of infectious complications during the post-transplant period. Understanding local outcomes is therefore essential for tailoring treatment protocols and facilitating evidence-based quality improvement.

We present a detailed analysis of the auto-HSCT programme for MM at the Department of Clinical Haematology and Bone Marrow Transplant, KIMSHEALTH, Thiruvananthapuram - one of the leading tertiary referral centres for haemato-oncology in South India. This retrospective analysis covers 16 consecutive patients transplanted between July 2023 and January 2026 and provides insights into patient characteristics, induction regimens, mobilisation, conditioning, engraftment kinetics, toxicity, and early response outcomes.

Patients and methods

Study design and setting

This is a single-centre retrospective cohort study conducted at the Department of Clinical Haematology and Bone Marrow Transplant, KIMSHEALTH Thiruvananthapuram, Kerala. The study period extended from July 2023 to January 2026. All patients who underwent auto-HSCT for MM during this period were included. Institutional ethical approval and patient consent were obtained.

Patient selection

Patients were included if they: (a) had a confirmed diagnosis of MM per International Myeloma Working Group (IMWG) criteria; (b) were transplant-eligible based on age (<70 years), Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) performance status ≤2, and adequate cardiac, pulmonary, hepatic, and renal function; (c) had received induction therapy with at least a partial response (PR) prior to transplantation; and (d) underwent successful stem cell collection yielding ≥2 × 106 CD34+ cells/kg.

Induction therapy

Induction regimens were selected based on clinical risk stratification, patient comorbidities, organ function, and available therapeutic access. VRd (bortezomib, lenalidomide, dexamethasone) served as the most commonly used regimen. Daratumumab was incorporated into frontline regimens in 4 of 16 patients (25%). Salvage regimens (VTD PACE, KPD+Cyclophosphamide) were used in patients with refractory disease prior to transplantation.

Stem cell mobilisation and collection

All patients underwent peripheral blood stem cell mobilisation using G-CSF (filgrastim) with plerixafor as a universal addition to the mobilisation protocol - a departure from selective plerixafor use seen in many international centres. CD34+ cells were collected by apheresis and the target was ≥4 × 106 CD34+ cells/kg when possible (minimum 2 × 106/kg).

Conditioning regimen

The conditioning chemotherapy comprised high-dose melphalan. Doses were individualized based on age, renal function, performance status, and body surface area. Three dose levels were employed: 200 mg/m² (standard), 160 mg/m² (intermediate), and 140 mg/m² (reduced intensity).

Supportive care and G-CSF

Post-transplant G-CSF was initiated on a median of day +3 (range D+2 to D+5). Standard antifungal, antibacterial, and antiviral prophylaxis was administered per institutional protocol. All patients received mucositis prophylaxis including cryotherapy and oral hygiene measures.

Response assessment

Response was assessed according to the 2016 IMWG criteria at D+90, D+180, D+365, and D+730 post-transplantation. Response categories included stringent complete response (sCR), very good partial response (VGPR), partial response (PR), and progressive disease (PD). Maintenance therapy was prescribed as singlet (lenalidomide) or doublet (lenalidomide + bortezomib) post-transplant.

Statistical analysis

Baseline characteristics were summarised using descriptive statistics. Response rates were reported as proportions. Progression-free survival (PFS) was calculated from the date of transplant to relapse, progression, or death. Owing to the small sample size and relatively short follow-up, formal Kaplan-Meier survival analyses were not performed but are planned for the updated dataset.

Results

Patient characteristics

Sixteen patients with MM underwent auto-HSCT at KIMSHEALTH during the study period (Table 1). All transplantations were autologous. The median age of cohort was 55 years, with the youngest patient who underwent transplantation being 34 years of age and oldest being 64 years of age. Of the total 16 patients, 10 were males and six were females. The disease profile reflected a predominantly intermediate-risk population with some high-risk features: 31.3% were R-ISS stage I, 50% stage II, and 18.7% stage III. The most common paraprotein subtype was IgA Kappa (31.3%), followed by IgA Lambda (25.0%) and IgG (25.0%). Light chain myeloma (Kappa LC) constituted 18.7%.

Lytic bone lesions were the most prevalent CRAB feature, present in 81.2% of patients, followed by anaemia (56.2%). Hypercalcaemia and renal failure were each present in 18.8%. Extramedullary disease (EMD) was documented in one patient (6.2%). Importantly, no patient had amyloidosis. High-risk cytogenetic abnormalities, including del(17p) and t(4;14), t(14;16) or others were documented in two patients (12.5%). The relatively low rate of documented high-risk cytogenetics may reflect incomplete FISH testing in the early phase of the programme.

Induction therapy and pre-transplant response

VRd was the most commonly used induction regimen, administered in seven patients (43.7%) (Table 2). Daratumumab-containing frontline regimens (Dara-VRd) were used in four patients (25%). KPD (carfilzomib-pomalidomide-dexamethasone) was used in two patients as later-line induction. The median number of pre-transplant cycles was four to seven, with most patients receiving four to six cycles before transplantation.

Before transplantation, the vast majority of patients (62.5%) had achieved sCR and 31.3% were in VGPR. Only one patient (6.2%) proceeded to transplant in PR. This excellent pre-transplant depth of response likely contributed to the high post-transplant sCR rates seen in this cohort, consistent with established literature demonstrating that deeper pre-transplant responses correlate with better post-transplant outcomes.6

One patient (R-ISS III) required VTD PACE (bortezomib, thalidomide, dexamethasone, cisplatin, doxorubicin, cyclophosphamide, etoposide) as a salvage regimen with daratumumab, reflecting the challenges of multi-refractory disease being taken to transplant. Despite achieving four lines of therapy, this patient achieved only VGPR pre-transplant and subsequently developed early PD post-transplant, underscoring the poor prognosis of this subgroup.

Stem cell mobilisation and graft characteristics

Plerixafor was used in all 16 patients (100%) as part of the mobilisation strategy — a deliberate institutional protocol choice to maximise CD34+ yield and minimise mobilisation failures (Table 3). This is in contrast to most international guidelines which recommend plerixafor selectively for poor mobilisers or as pre-emptive strategy based on CD34+ peripheral blood counts.7 The rationale at KIMSHEALTH reflects both the logistical constraints of apheresis scheduling and the goal of achieving an optimal stem cell graft with adequate reserve for potential second transplant.

The median CD34+ yield was 7.80 × 106/kg (range 2.49-13.0 × 106/kg), substantially exceeding the minimum threshold of 2 × 106/kg and the target of 4 × 106/kg for most patients. The lowest yield (2.49 × 106/kg) was seen in the patient with multi-refractory disease who had received the most prior therapies. This demonstrates the well-established inverse relationship between prior therapy burden and stem cell yield.

Melphalan 200 mg/m² was used in seven patients (43.7%) as standard conditioning, while dose-reduced melphalan at 160 mg/m² and 140 mg/m² was used in four (25.0%) and five (31.3%) patients respectively. Dose reduction was based on age, comorbidities, and renal function, consistent with evidence-based practice. The IFM 2014-01 trial and subsequent analyses have validated the continued superiority of Mel200 in fit patients, while supporting Mel140 in older or renally compromised individuals.8

Engraftment kinetics

All 16 patients achieved engraftment. Median neutrophil engraftment occurred on D+11 (range D+8 to D+13), and median platelet engraftment on D+14 (range D+8 to D+23). One patient had delayed platelet engraftment, attributed to prolonged cytopenia in the context of post-transplant infectious complications. These engraftment timelines are consistent with international published data for auto-HSCT in MM with plerixafor-assisted mobilisation.9

Notably, higher CD34+ yields correlated with earlier engraftment in several patients.

Toxicity profile

The transplant period was universally complicated by febrile neutropenia (100%), reflecting the expected post-engraftment immunosuppression (Table 4). Mucositis was predominantly grade 2 (62.5%), with 5 patients (31.3%) experiencing grade 3 mucositis. No grade 4 mucositis or transplant-related mortality from mucositis-associated sepsis was recorded.

Diarrhoea was present in 93.8% of patients, with grade 1 diarrhoea in 56.3% and grade 2 diarrhoea in 37.5%. MDRO (multi-drug-resistant organism) infections were documented in two patients (12.5%), highlighting the increasing concern of resistant nosocomial infections in the transplant setting, particularly relevant to tertiary centres in South India where MDRO rates are substantially higher than Western cohorts.10

Response assessment

Response rates demonstrated progressive deepening over time, a characteristic pattern of auto-HSCT in MM (Table 5). At D+90, 73.3% of evaluable patients achieved sCR, with a cumulative ≥VGPR rate of 86.7%. At D+180, the sCR rate improved further to 83.3%, with ≥VGPR in 91.7%. One patient with multiple lines refractory R-ISS III disease developed progressive disease by day +90.

At D+365, seven patients had evaluable data (reflecting that several transplants occurred in 2025-2026 and have not yet reached the 1-year timepoint). Among evaluable patients, 71.4% maintained sCR, and one patient showed response decline from sCR to PR at D+365, consistent with a late relapse pattern. At D+730, only one patient was evaluable, who maintained sCR, reflecting the excellent durability achievable with post-transplant maintenance in standard-risk MM.

Maintenance therapy

Post-transplant maintenance was prescribed in 14 of 16 patients for whom maintenance data were recorded. Singlet maintenance (lenalidomide) was used in 10 patients (71.4%) and doublet maintenance (lenalidomide + bortezomib) in four patients (28.6%). The choice of maintenance was influenced by pre-transplant response depth, risk stratification, and tolerability. Two patients did not receive maintenance therapy: one died before maintenance initiation and the other developed progressive disease before maintenance could be started.

The MYELOMA XI, IFM 2012-03, and FORTE trials have established lenalidomide maintenance as the standard of care post-ASCT in transplant-eligible MM, demonstrating significant PFS and, in some analyses, OS benefit.11 Doublet maintenance with bortezomib plus lenalidomide was preferred in patients with high-risk cytogenetics, PR response at transplantation or required multiple lines of therapy to achieve initial response pre-transplantation.

Discussion

Contextualising outcomes in the global landscape

The results from our centre's auto-HSCT programme for MM are encouraging and broadly align with outcomes reported from major transplant centres globally. The D+90 sCR rate of 73.3% and ≥VGPR rate of 86.7% in our cohort compares favourably with rates reported from landmark trials and real-world registries. The IFM 2009 trial reported post-ASCT sCR rates of approximately 46% (though post-consolidation), while GRIFFIN and CASSIOPEIA trials with daratumumab-based quadruplet induction demonstrated sCR rates approaching 50-60% post-transplant.12

Our higher-than-expected sCR rates likely reflect several factors: (1) an aggressive policy of targeting sCR/CR pre-transplant with extended induction cycles; (2) a relatively young cohort of transplant-eligible patients; and (3) possible under-ascertainment of MRD positivity, which, if assessed, might have reclassified some sCR patients as MRD-positive sCR — a distinction increasingly recognised as prognostically important.13

The engraftment kinetics observed (neutrophil D+11 and platelet D+14) are well within the expected range for auto-HSCT with melphalan conditioning and peripheral blood stem cell grafts. The universal use of plerixafor likely contributed to the robust CD34+ cell yields (median 7.8 × 106/kg), which in turn may have accelerated engraftment in patients with highest yields.

The role of daratumumab in frontline therapy

Twenty-five percent of patients in our cohort received daratumumab as part of frontline induction — a practice increasingly supported by emerging evidence. The GRIFFIN trial (VRd vs. Dara-VRd) demonstrated significantly higher MRD-negative CR rates with the daratumumab quadruplet (42.4% vs. 32.0%), and the PERSEUS trial subsequently confirmed a PFS advantage for Dara-VRd maintained with daratumumab-lenalidomide.14

All four patients who received daratumumab-containing frontline regimens achieved sCR before transplantation and have either maintained sCR post-transplant or continue to be followed. This observation is consistent with the biological rationale that daratumumab's CD38-targeting mechanism complements PI and IMiD activity, resulting in deeper clonal cytoreduction and potentially MRD negativity that translates to durable post-transplant remission.

The Indian transplant context and infectious challenges

The 100% febrile neutropenia rate and 12.5% MDRO rate in our cohort merit specific discussion in the Indian context. Febrile neutropenia following auto-HSCT is expected and manageable; however, MDRO infections represent an escalating challenge. A multicentre Indian study by Bhattacharya et al. reported MDRO bacteraemia rates of 30-40% in hematological malignancy wards, with carbapenem-resistant Enterobacteriaceae (CRE) and Acinetobacter baumannii predominating.10 Our 12.5% rate, while lower, nevertheless reflects the ongoing challenge.

Strategies to mitigate MDRO burden in Indian transplant units include: (1) rigorous contact precautions and environmental decontamination; (2) antimicrobial stewardship programs; (3) selective bowel decontamination (which remains controversial but is used in some high-risk centres); (4) early identification and cohorting of MDRO-positive patients; and (5) phage therapy or novel beta-lactam/beta-lactamase inhibitor combinations for resistant organisms.15

The death of one patient from infectious complications underscores that even in an era of effective antimicrobials, infection remains a major cause of non-relapse mortality in the Indian transplant setting. Post-transplant immune reconstitution in myeloma is also adversely affected by the underlying disease and prior therapies, contributing to prolonged susceptibility to infection.

Response deepening and the concept of clonal extinction

The progressive deepening of response from D+90 to D+180 observed in our cohort — with improvement in the sCR rate from 73.3% to 83.3% — illustrates the phenomenon of ongoing clonal cytoreduction after auto-HSCT in the presence of maintenance therapy. This phenomenon is well-documented and forms part of the biological rationale for post-HSCT maintenance, wherein continued lenalidomide exposure eliminates residual myeloma clones escaping the melphalan-induced eradication.11

The clinical relevance of achieving MRD negativity by next-generation flow (NGF) or next-generation sequencing (NGS) is increasingly recognised; however, MRD assessment was not routinely performed in our cohort. Future protocol iterations at KIMSHEALTH should incorporate systematic MRD testing at D+100 post-ASCT and before and after maintenance initiation, as this will provide critical prognostic data and potentially guide maintenance duration.

Prognostication and high-risk features

R-ISS staging at diagnosis appropriately stratified our cohort. The single case of progressive disease at D+90 (R-ISS III, 4 prior lines, VTD PACE conditioning regimen) illustrates the adverse prognosis of multi-refractory, late-presenting high-risk MM even with ASCT. For such patients, novel approaches including bispecific antibodies (teclistamab, talquetamab), CAR-T cell therapy (idecabtagene vicleucel, ciltacabtagene autoleucel), or early allografting in select cases may need consideration.16

High-risk cytogenetics (del17p, t(4;14), t(14;16), 1q21 amplification) were identified in only two patients (12.5%), which likely reflects incomplete fluorescence in situ hybridisation (FISH) panel testing due to outsourcing of tests (which may affect the quality of sample processed) rather than true population prevalence. Comprehensive cytogenetic assessment using standard FISH panels is now recommended in all NDMM patients and will be systematically captured in future KIMSHEALTH datasets.

Limitations

This analysis is limited by: (1) the small sample size (n=16); (2) retrospective design with inherent selection and ascertainment biases; (3) absence of MRD data; (4) incomplete long-term follow-up for recently transplanted patients; (5) single-centre design limiting generalisability. The program is growing, and updated analyses with larger cohorts, standardised MRD assessment, and prospective data collection are planned.

Conclusions

The auto-HSCT programme for MM at KIMSHEALTH, Thiruvananthapuram has successfully established a robust operational framework delivering outcomes comparable to international benchmarks. The key highlights from this 16-patient cohort are:

  • Universal use of plerixafor delivers excellent median CD34+ yields (7.80 × 106/kg) with 100% mobilisation success.
  • Rapid and reliable engraftment was achieved: neutrophil D+11, platelet D+14.
  • High rates of deep pre-transplant response were observed: 62.5% sCR, 31.3% VGPR before HSCT.
  • Excellent post-transplant responses were noted: D+90 sCR 73.3%, ≥VGPR 86.7%; D+180 sCR 83.3%.
  • Toxicities were manageable, with no grade 4 mucositis observed. MDRO infections remain an area for improvement.
  • Incorporation of daratumumab into 25% of frontline regimens reflects the adoption of contemporary treatment practices.

Future directions include systematic MRD testing, standardised FISH panel cytogenetics, prospective data capture, and expansion of the program with potential for tandem transplantation in selected high-risk patients. Continued expansion of the KIMSHEALTH Haematology & BMT program and prospective outcome monitoring will help strengthen its role in delivering comprehensive myeloma care in the region.

articles.title: External validation of the Sudbury Vertigo Risk Score in acute vertigo: a retrospective cohort study from a South Indian tertiary emergency department

affiliations.text: Department of Emergency Medicine, KIMSHEALTH, Trivandrum, Kerala, India.

abstract.heading: Background
abstract.text: Acute vertigo accounts for 5-10% of emergency department (ED) visits globally. Differentiating central from peripheral aetiology remains diagnostically challenging. The Sudbury Vertigo Risk Score (SVRS), developed in Canadian EDs, has not been validated in South Asian populations.

abstract.heading: Objectives
abstract.text: To retrospectively validate the SVRS for risk stratification of central versus peripheral vertigo in a South Indian tertiary ED using MRI-confirmed outcomes.

abstract.heading: Methods
abstract.text: This retrospective cohort study used electronic medical record (EMR) data at KIMSHEALTH ED, Thiruvananthapuram, collected between January and December 2025. The sample size (n=206) was power-calculated based on the parent Canadian SVRS study (AUROC 0.81, α=0.05, power 80%, prevalence 23%). A stratified random sample was extracted from 876 eligible records. SVRS was calculated retrospectively from EMR-documented clinical data. The reference standard was MRI Brain with diffusion weighted imaging (DWI) and apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) sequences interpreted by neurologists blinded to the study hypothesis.

abstract.heading: Results
abstract.text: Of 1,187 records screened, 206 were included. Central aetiology was confirmed in 23% (n=47). SVRS AUROC 0.86 (95% CI: 0.80-0.91). At optimal threshold (SVRS >8), sensitivity was 91.3%, specificity 77.9%, LR+ 4.13, and LR− 0.11. MRI positivity was 0% (low <5), 4.2% (moderate 5-8), and 55.3% (high >8; p<0.001).

abstract.heading: Conclusions
abstract.text: The SVRS demonstrated excellent diagnostic performance (AUROC 0.86) in a South Indian ED. This study represents the first retrospective external validation of the SVRS in an Indian setting. The tool is simple, requires no equipment, and immediately deployable and may facilitate more rational use of neuroimaging while reducing missed diagnoses of central vertigo.

Introduction

Stroke is among the leading causes of death and disability worldwide. The Global Burden of Disease Study 2019 estimated over 12 million new stroke cases annually, with the majority occurring in low- and middle-income countries.1 India bears a disproportionate burden, with a crude stroke incidence of 108-172 per 100,000 population per year, and hypertension identified as the single most attributable modifiable risk factor.2

Posterior circulation stroke accounts for 20-25% of all ischaemic strokes and frequently presents with acute vertigo, a symptom shared with numerous benign peripheral vestibular disorders. Central causes are responsible for 20-35% of acute vertigo presentations in tertiary EDs, and reliance on clinical gestalt alone results in missed central diagnoses in approximately 35% of cases, even among experienced physicians.3

Existing clinical decision tools carry significant limitations in the Indian context. The HINTS examination (Head Impulse, Nystagmus, Test of Skew) has been widely used in ED practice.4 The ABCD² score, originally designed for transient ischaemic attack (TIA) risk stratification, performs poorly in posterior circulation events.5 Importantly, no risk stratification tool has been externally validated in Indian or South Asian populations, where the high prevalence of hypertension and diabetes may substantially alter pre-test probability of central vertigo.

The Sudbury Vertigo Risk Score (SVRS) was developed by Glover et al. and subsequently validated in a Canadian multicentre cohort.6,7 The seven-component score incorporates vascular risk factors - male sex (+1), age >65 (+1), diabetes (+1), hypertension (+3) - and neurological findings including motor or sensory deficits (+5), cerebellar signs (+6), and benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (−5). Scores <5 indicate low stroke probability, scores 5-8 moderate risk, and scores >8 high risk warranting urgent neuroimaging. To date, the SVRS has not been externally validated in South Asian populations. Therefore, this study aimed to retrospectively validate the SVRS in a high-volume South Indian ED, evaluate its diagnostic performance against MRI-confirmed outcomes, and characterise MRI positivity rates across risk categories.

Methods

Study design and setting

We conducted a retrospective observational cohort study using routinely collected electronic medical record (EMR) data at the Emergency Department of KIMSHEALTH, a tertiary care center with 24/7 CT, MRI, neurology, and an advanced stroke program. The study period was from January 1 to December 31, 2025. Institutional Ethics Committee approval was obtained with waiver of individual patient consent because the study involved analysis of pre-existing clinical records.

Participants and sample size

Eligible participants were adults aged ≥18 years presenting to the ED with acute vertigo or dizziness within a 72-hour duration. They were identified from ED EMR records. Exclusion criteria included trauma, known intracranial pathology, systolic blood <90 mmHg; Glasgow Coma Scale <15, non-vestibular dizziness (example, hypoglycaemia, sepsis), or incomplete documentation precluding SVRS calculation.

Sample size and data collection

Sample size was power-calculated from the parent Canadian SVRS study,5 (Expected AUROC 0.81, α=0.05, power 80%, central prevalence 23% minimum n=196.) The minimum required sample size (196 patients) was calculated using the Hanley-McNeil method. A target sample size (of n=206) was set for 5% data-loss allowance. Among 876 eligible records, a stratified random sample based on symptom severity (mild, moderate, and severe) was selected to ensure representative sampling.

The SVRS (Table 1) was calculated retrospectively using clinical data documented at the time of ED presentation, before imaging or specialist review. Component data (neurological signs, vascular risk factors, Dix-Hallpike result) were obtained from structured EMR fields. The reference standard was MRI Brain with DWI/ADC sequences, performed as part of routine clinical care. Table 1 presents SVRS scoring components.

Statistical analyses used SPSS version 26 and MedCalc version 20. AUROC was calculated using DeLong's method (95% CI). The optimal threshold was identified using Youden's Index (J = sensitivity + specificity − 1). Sensitivity, specificity, PPV, NPV, and likelihood ratios (LR+, LR−) were calculated with 95% CIs by Wilson's method. MRI positivity across SVRS risk categories was compared by Pearson's chi-square. Pre-specified subgroup analyses evaluated performance according to age (≥65 vs <65), hypertension, diabetes, and sex. A p value <0.05 was considered statistically significant.

Results

Baseline characteristics

Of 1,187 ED records screened, 876 met eligibility criteria, and a stratified random sample of 206 patients was extracted (Figure 1). Mean age was 58.4 ± 13.2 years; 52% were female; 50% were aged ≥65. Hypertension was present in 56% of patients and diabetes in 48.5%. Neurological findings included motor or sensory deficit in 44.7%, cerebellar signs in 43.2%, and positive Dix-Hallpike in 39%. Final diagnoses were peripheral vertigo in 159 patients (77%) and central causes in 47 patients (23%). Baseline characteristics are presented in Table 2.

Diagnostic performance

The SVRS demonstrated excellent discriminatory ability for identifying central causes of vertigo, with an AUROC of 0.86 (95% CI: 0.80-0.91) (Figure 2). At the optimal threshold (SVRS >8; Youden's J=0.683), sensitivity was 91.3% (95% CI: 79.2-97.6%) and specificity was 77.9% (95% CI: 71.1-83.7%). LR+ was 4.13 (95% CI: 3.01-5.66) and LR− 0.11 (95% CI: 0.04-0.28). Full metrics across thresholds are in Table 3.

MRI positivity by risk category

MRI positivity increased progressively (p<0.001), from 0% in the low-risk group (SVRS <5; n=65) to 4.2% in moderate-risk (SVRS 5-8; n=63), and 55.3% in high-risk (SVRS >8; n=78). Results are presented in Table 4 and Figure 3.

Subgroup analyses

The AUROC ranged from 0.81 among patients age <65 to 0.91 in patients with cerebellar signs across all pre-specified subgroups, with no significant interaction effects detected (all p>0.1). Performance was notably higher in hypertensive patients (AUROC 0.88) and those with diabetes (AUROC 0.85), consistent with the +3 weighting of hypertension in the SVRS. No significant interaction effects were observed across the pre-specified subgroups (all p>0.10). Performance remained robust among patients with hypertension (AUROC 0.88) and diabetes mellitus (AUROC 0.85).

Discussion

This retrospective study represents the first external validation of the SVRS in a South Asian ED population. The score demonstrated robust discriminatory performance, with an AUROC of 0.86, comparable to or exceeding both the original Canadian derivation cohort (AUROC 0.81) and subsequent Canadian validation (AUROC 0.82). At the optimal threshold, a sensitivity of 91.3% is clinically meaningful. In acute vertigo, where missed central causes carry substantial neurological risk, correctly identifying more than 90% of central cases markedly outperforms unaided clinical judgement, which may miss up to one-third of central presentations.3

The stepwise gradient in MRI positivity—0%, 4.2%, and 55.3% across low-, moderate-, and high-risk strata—is the most clinically compelling finding of this study. The absence of MRI-positive cases in the low-risk group (SVRS <5) provides empirical support for safe discharge without routine neuroimaging, corroborating the original Canadian data6 and extending this finding to an Indian ED population. Conversely, the 55.3% MRI positivity rate in the high-risk group far exceeds published ED MRI yields from unguided ED practice (2-15%),8 reinforcing the validity of SVRS-based risk stratification. Based on our cohort distribution, SVRS-guided triage could reduce inappropriate neuroimaging by approximately 31%, while simultaneously directing MRI resources toward patients with the highest diagnostic yield.

The SVRS offers several advantages over existing tools in the Indian ED context. Unlike the HINTS, it does not require specialist training or neuro-otological expertise, an important consideration given that most Indian EDs lack immediate access to vestibular specialists.4 Unlike ABCD², the SVRS was specifically designed for vertigo risk stratification and incorporates neurological findings with clinically appropriate weighting: cerebellar signs (+6) and motor/sensory deficits (+5) dominate the composite score, capturing the neurological signatures most predictive of posterior circulation pathology.5 The score can be completed at triage in under two minutes by any trained resident, making it immediately deployable across resource-variable Indian ED settings.

The contribution of the hypertension component (+3) is notable in our cohort, where hypertension prevalence (56%) was substantially higher than in the Canadian derivation population. The SVRS appears well-calibrated for South Asian vascular risk patterns, where hypertension-related cerebrovascular disease is the dominant mechanism of posterior circulation stroke.8 Enhanced subgroup performance in hypertensive patients (AUROC 0.88) supports this observation. The high prevalence of diabetes (48.5%) further underscores the tool's relevance in populations with elevated metabolic risk and higher pre-test probability of central vertigo.

Comparison with other tools applied to the same cohort reinforces the superiority of the SVRS. HINTS demonstrated inferior AUROC (0.78 vs 0.86; p=0.009), consistent with its reduced accuracy in non-specialist hands. ABCD² performed poorly (AUROC 0.68), as expected given its derivation for TIA rather than vertigo-specific risk assessment.4 The STANDING algorithm performed better (AUROC 0.75), but requires multi-step serial assessment and lacks validation outside European populations.9

Limitations

Several limitations of the retrospective design must be acknowledged. First, SVRS was calculated from EMR documentation, introducing potential documentation bias, particularly for neurological signs recorded with variable rigour by different clinicians. Second, this single-centre study from a quaternary academic ED may not be generalisable to community or district-level hospitals. Third, while the stratified sample of 206 patients was adequately powered for the primary AUROC analysis, secondary subgroup metrics carry wider confidence intervals and should be interpreted cautiously. Fourth, cases where Dix-Hallpike testing was not performed were classified as BPPV-negative by default, potentially introducing misclassification bias. Fifth, long-term neurological outcomes were not captured. Nonetheless, the retrospective design allowed evaluation of the SVRS in a real-world, uncontrolled clinical environment, free from the Hawthorne effect that may influence prospective studies.10 Future priorities include multicentre prospective validation, a pragmatic randomised trial comparing SVRS-guided versus standard neuroimaging strategies, and automated integration of the SVRS into electronic triage systems.

Conclusion

In this retrospective South Indian ED cohort, the Sudbury Vertigo Risk Score demonstrated excellent discriminatory performance (AUROC 0.86), high sensitivity (91.3%), and a clinically meaningful stepwise increase in MRI positivity across risk categories. The study provides the first external retrospective validation of the SVRS in an Indian ED population. The score is simple, objective, equipment-free, and immediately deployable at triage, making it a practical tool for rationalising neuroimaging, reducing inappropriate CT/MRI use, and improving early identification of central vertigo across Indian Emergency Medicine. Multicentre validation across diverse ED settings is now warranted to confirm generalisability.

abstract.heading: Background
abstract.text: Pre-operative echocardiography (ECHO) is increasingly requested before non-cardiac surgeries, despite evidence questioning its routine use in low-risk patients. This audit evaluated the appropriateness of ECHO referrals, echocardiographic findings, and their clinical impact on perioperative management in a tertiary care center.

abstract.heading: Methods
abstract.text: This retrospective cross-sectional clinical audit included 150 consecutive patients who underwent pre-operative ECHO at KIMSHEALTH between January 2022 and July 2024. Referral pathways, ECHO findings, patient demographics, comorbidities, and post-operative complications were analyzed and assessed for adherence to the American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association/American Society of Echocardiography and British Society of Echocardiography guidelines.

abstract.heading: Results
abstract.text: Most ECHO referrals (86.6%) originated directly from primary consultants, bypassing the pre-anesthesia check-up (PAC) pathway. Nearly two-thirds of referrals (64.7%) lacked a specific cardiac indication. More than half of the examinations (55.3%) were normal, and only 6.7% resulted in further evaluation or management. Post-operative complications occurred in 4% of patients, and 83.3% had completely normal pre-operative ECHO findings.

abstract.heading: Conclusion
abstract.text: Routine pre-operative ECHO in young, low-risk patients offers limited clinical yield and poor predictive value for post-operative adverse events. PAC-driven referral pathways and institutionally endorsed evidence-based protocols may help refine resource utilization.

articles.bodyHtml:
Introduction

Echocardiography is a versatile, non-invasive cardiac imaging modality that has become indispensable for the evaluation of structural and functional heart disease. In the pre-operative setting, it provides detailed information about ventricular function, valvular pathology, and hemodynamic status — data that can meaningfully influence anesthetic and surgical planning in selected high-risk patients.

However, current evidence and international guidelines recommend pre-operative ECHO only for specific clinical indications, including known or suspected structural heart disease, unexplained dyspnea or reduced exercise tolerance, significant arrhythmias, or chronic kidney disease with hemodynamic sequelae. In clinically low-risk patients proceeding to elective non-cardiac surgery, routine pre-operative ECHO increases costs, contributes to administrative burden, and may cause unnecessary delays without enhancing patient safety.1,2 At KIMSHEALTH, Thiruvananthapuram, a tertiary referral center with a busy surgical program encompassing multiple specialties, echocardiograms are frequently requested as part of pre-operative evaluation. Anecdotal observations from the Department of Cardiology suggested that a significant proportion of these referrals, mainly among younger patients without established cardiovascular comorbidities, may not conform to evidence-based recommendations for investigation.

This audit was undertaken to evaluate the appropriateness of pre-operative ECHO referrals, describe the profile of patients undergoing the investigation, determine the clinical yield of ECHO findings, and assess their impact on perioperative management and post-operative outcomes. The main objective was to establish a structured, guideline-concordant referral pathway that optimizes resource utilization without jeopardizing patient safety.

Standards and benchmarks

The audit standards were derived from the following evidence-based recommendations:

  • American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association/American Society of Echocardiography (ACC/AHA/ASE) Guideline Update for the Clinical Application of Echocardiography (2003), which outlines appropriate indications for echocardiography in perioperative cardiovascular evaluation.1
  • British Society of Echocardiography (BSE) guidelines on the appropriate use of transthoracic echocardiography in adult patients.2
  • UpToDate recommendations on pre-operative cardiac evaluation for non-cardiac surgery.3

These standards consistently recommend that pre-operative echocardiography should be reserved for patients in whom cardiac pathology is known, suspected on clinical grounds, or likely to alter perioperative management. They do not support the routine use of ECHO as a general fitness-for-surgery investigation tool.

Methodology

Study design

This retrospective cross-sectional clinical audit was conducted at the Department of Cardiology, KIMSHEALTH, Thiruvananthapuram, over a 30-month period from January 2022 to July 2024.

Study population

A total of 150 patients who underwent pre-operative echocardiography before non-cardiac surgery or invasive procedures were included. Patients were identified through electronic medical records, anesthesia logs, and cardiology reporting systems.

Inclusion criteria

  • Patients undergoing non-cardiac surgery or invasive procedures under general anesthesia or monitored sedation.
  • A pre-operative ECHO performed within 90 days of the planned procedure.
  • Referral for ECHO based on ECG abnormality, suspected cardiac disease, or surgical fitness assessment.

Exclusion criteria

  • Patients undergoing cardiac surgeries.
  • Patients with previously diagnosed structural heart disease undergoing routine ECHO surveillance.
  • Patients with incomplete medical records.

Data collection

The following parameters were systematically extracted from electronic medical records and analyzed:

  • Patient characteristics: age, sex, body mass index (where available).
  • Comorbidities: hypertension, diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease, ischemic heart disease, arrhythmias.
  • Referral source: Referrals originating through the pre-anesthesia checkup (PAC) process versus those initiated directly by the primary admitting team.
  • Indication for ECHO: Documented cardiac indications (including abnormal ECG, suspected structural heart disease, arrhythmia) versus requests made solely for pre-operative fitness assessment without a specific cardiac indication.
  • Echocardiographic findings: normal findings, minor abnormalities with no management change, and clinically significant abnormalities warranting additional cardiac assessment or management.
  • Perioperative outcomes: Post-operative complications occurring within 30 days of the procedure, including atrial fibrillation (AF), supraventricular tachycardia (SVT), ventricular premature complexes (VPC), or other cardiac events.

Results

Patient demographics and referral characteristics

The audit cohort comprised 150 patients. Table 1 summarises the key demographic and referral characteristics.

The most striking finding in referral pattern analysis was that only 13.4% of all ECHO requests were generated through the Pre-Anaesthesia Checkup — the pathway recommended by guidelines as the appropriate screening filter before cardiac investigations are requested. The overwhelming majority (86.6%) were initiated directly by the primary admitting surgical or medical team, often without a documented cardiac indication.

The 20-40 age group accounted for 28% of all referrals. Among patients without any documented comorbidity (n=66), 39 still underwent echocardiography — a group in whom international guidelines generally do not recommend the investigation.

Echocardiographic findings

Table 2 presents the distribution of echocardiographic findings across the cohort.

Over half of all echocardiograms were entirely normal (55.3%). A further 38% demonstrated minor abnormalities — including mild diastolic dysfunction, trivial valvular regurgitation, or borderline wall motion — that did not result in any change to the planned anesthetic or surgical approach. Only 6.7% of studies identified findings that materially altered perioperative management, such as moderate-to-severe valvular disease, significant ventricular dysfunction, or previously unrecognized structural abnormality warranting further evaluation or optimization prior to surgery.

This clinical yield of approximately 1 in 15 referrals significantly changes management and underscores the low value of non-selective, routine pre-operative ECHO in this population.

Post-operative complications

Post-operative cardiac complications were recorded in 6 patients (4% of the cohort). The nature and pre-operative ECHO status of these cases are summarised in Table 3.

83.3% of patients who developed post-operative complications had a completely normal pre-operative echocardiogram, while the remaining patient had a minor abnormality that had not prompted any change in management.

Discussion

This audit documents a significant pattern of guideline-discordant ECHO referral practice at KIMSHEALTH during the study period. Nearly two-thirds of echocardiograms were requested for surgical fitness assessment in the absence of a specific cardiac indication — a practice not supported by any major international guideline. The audit also demonstrates that current referral pathways overwhelmingly bypass the Pre-Anaesthesia Checkup, the clinical checkpoint most appropriately positioned to triage the need for cardiac investigations before non-cardiac surgery.

The demographic data reveal a particularly concerning sub-pattern: a substantial proportion of ECHOs were performed in patients aged 20-40 years, the very age group in whom the pre-test probability of clinically relevant cardiac disease is lowest, and in whom incidental minor findings are most likely to generate diagnostic uncertainty, further unnecessary investigation, or even procedural delays without benefit.

Consistent with other published clinical audits in similar healthcare settings, our data confirm that the large majority of pre-operative echocardiograms in unselected patients yield either normal or clinically inconsequential findings.4 More importantly, in this cohort, post-operative complications occurred predominantly in patients with a normal pre-operative ECHO. Although the small number of events (n=6) precludes any firm conclusion about predictive performance, this observation is consistent with the broader literature suggesting that routine ECHO should not be relied upon as a general safety net for perioperative risk in unselected patients. This limited predictive value does not appear to reflect a flaw in echocardiographic interpretation, but rather a mismatch between the investigation's intended purpose — detection of structural and functional cardiac disease — and its frequent use here as a general screening tool for surgical fitness.

The ACC/AHA/ASE guidelines have long distinguished between appropriate and inappropriate uses of echocardiography in the pre-operative context. The indications that most consistently offer clinical value include: evaluation of unexplained dyspnoea prior to major surgery, assessment of known or suspected valvular disease, characterization of ventricular function in patients with heart failure symptoms, and risk stratification in patients with high-risk comorbidities such as CKD stage 4-5 or pulmonary hypertension.1 These are also the precise scenarios in which PAC-based triage is most likely to identify appropriate candidates.

From a resource utilization and healthcare efficiency standpoint, the finding that 97 referrals (64.7%) lacked a documented cardiac indication carries meaningful cost and capacity implications over the 30-month audit period — particularly in the context of the increasing demand on echocardiography laboratory capacity for genuinely indicated studies such as valvular surveillance, cardiomyopathy monitoring, and hemodynamic assessment in patients with complex cardiovascular disease.

Recommendations

Based on the findings of this audit, the following evidence-based recommendations are proposed for adoption by the Departments of Cardiology, Anaesthesiology, and Surgery at KIMSHEALTH:

  1. Mandate PAC-based referral pathways for all pre-operative ECHO requests: The Pre-Anaesthesia Checkup should serve as the exclusive primary gateway for ECHO referrals before non-cardiac surgery. Direct referrals from surgical teams without PAC clearance should be formally discouraged and systematically tracked.
  2. Restrict routine ECHO in patients aged 20-40 without cardiac comorbidities: In the absence of an abnormal ECG, documented cardiovascular disease, unexplained dyspnoea, or significant risk factors, ECHO should not be reflexively ordered in this age group.
  3. Develop and implement an institutional pre-operative ECHO indication protocol: A standardized, locally endorsed algorithmic checklist — aligned with ACC/AHA/BSE guidance — should be developed, approved by the relevant departmental heads, and integrated into the hospital information system's pre-operative order sets.
  4. Establish a prospective data registry for pre-operative ECHO referrals: Tracking of referral source, indication, finding, and surgical outcome should be systematized to enable a robust longitudinal audit.

Action plan and follow-up

Following the presentation of this audit to the Cardiology and Anaesthesiology departments, the following actions have been initiated:

  • Multidisciplinary meeting held with anaesthesiologists and senior surgical residents to discuss the findings and the rationale for revised referral pathways.
  • Draft institutional protocol for pre-operative ECHO referrals submitted to the Department of Cardiology for review.
  • Communication circulated to surgical departments outlining the evidence base for appropriate ECHO utilization.

Conclusion

This clinical audit provides robust institutional evidence that preoperative echocardiography is widely overutilized in the context of non-cardiac surgery at KIMSHEALTH. The majority of requests are generated outside recommended referral pathways, in patient populations where clinical yield is low, and management impact is minimal. Critically, the practice does not meaningfully predict post-operative cardiac complications.

A structural change in referral culture — anchored in PAC-based triage and an evidence-based institutional protocol — is both necessary and achievable. Implementing such changes will improve resource allocation, reduce unnecessary delays in surgical scheduling for low-risk patients, and redirect echocardiography laboratory capacity towards high-value, clinically indicated studies.

This audit reaffirms that clinical utility, not reflexive habit, should drive pre-operative investigation — and that evidence-based resource stewardship is an integral component of quality cardiology practice.

articles.title: Knowledge and attitudes towards antimicrobial resistance among nursing students: A cross-sectional study

affiliations.text: KIMS College of Nursing, Trivandrum, Kerala, India.

abstract.text: Antimicrobial resistance occurs when microorganisms such as bacteria, viruses, fungi, and parasites evolve and become resistant to the drugs designed to kill them. This study aimed to assess the knowledge and attitudes of nursing students regarding antimicrobial resistance (AMR) and its effects, determine the correlation between knowledge and attitude, and examine the association between knowledge and selected socio-personal variables (age, gender, religion, area of residence, and previous knowledge regarding AMR). A descriptive cross-sectional study was conducted among 100 nursing students at KIMS College of Nursing, Thiruvananthapuram, selected using non-probability purposive sampling. Data were collected after obtaining informed consent using a structured questionnaire comprising 25 multiple-choice questions to assess knowledge and a 5-point Likert scale to assess attitudes towards AMR. The results showed that 13% of the participants had poor knowledge, 32% had average knowledge, and 55% had good knowledge regarding antimicrobial resistance. All participants demonstrated a positive attitude towards AMR and its prevention. A statistically significant association was observed between knowledge and previous knowledge regarding AMR. However, no significant association was found between knowledge and other socio-personal variables such as gender, religion, and area of residence.

articles.bodyHtml:
Introduction

Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) has emerged as one of the major public health challenges of the 21st century, threatening the effective prevention and treatment of an increasing range of infections caused by bacteria, parasites, viruses, and fungi that have become resistant to commonly used antimicrobial agents.1

The development and spread of antimicrobial resistance in hospitals are driven by several factors, including poor infection control practices and selective pressure resulting from the overuse and misuse of antibiotics. Compliance with hand hygiene practices is often limited by the time required for handwashing and the adverse effects of repeated washing on the skin. Alcohol-based hand rubs help overcome these barriers and improve skin condition, while universal glove use can compensate for gaps in hand hygiene adherence. Among various interventions, antimicrobial stewardship programs that restrict inappropriate antibiotic use are among the most effective measures for controlling antimicrobial resistance.2

A study evaluating global trends in antibiotic consumption between 2016 and 2023, with projections up to 2030, demonstrated that total antibiotic consumption in 67 countries increased by 16.3%, from 29.5 to 34.3 billion defined daily doses (DDDs). During the same period, the antibiotic consumption rate increased by 10.6%, from 13.7 to 15.2 DDDs per 1,000 inhabitants per day.3

The first global surveillance report on antibiotic resistance, published by the World Health Organization (WHO), highlighted the clinical impact of resistant bacteria across WHO regions. Five of the six WHO regions reported resistance rates exceeding 50% to third-generation cephalosporins and fluoroquinolones in Escherichia coli, as well as methicillin resistance in Staphylococcus aureus in hospital settings.4 Several resistant bacterial pathogens have increasingly been implicated in human infections, particularly Enterococcus species, Staphylococcus aureus, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Acinetobacter baumannii, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and Enterobacter species.5

A community-based cross-sectional study conducted among primary school children and prisoners in Jimma Town, Southwest Ethiopia, reported an overall methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) prevalence of 23.1% (39/169). The prevalence was 18.8% (27/144) among school children and 48% (12/25) among prisoners. Both S. aureus and MRSA isolates exhibited multidrug resistance to two to ten antibiotics.6

According to the World Health Organization, antimicrobial resistance poses a substantial burden in India. In 2019, approximately 4.95 million deaths were associated with drug-resistant infections, of which 1.27 million deaths were directly attributable to AMR. One in five of these deaths occurred among children under five years of age. The major pathogens contributing to the burden in India include Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Staphylococcus aureus, Acinetobacter baumannii, and Mycobacterium tuberculosis.7 In Kerala, antimicrobial resistance is an emerging public health concern. A report published by the Kerala Antimicrobial Resistance Surveillance Network (KARS-NET) and highlighted in The Hindu in 2023 indicated an increasing trend in carbapenem and other broad-spectrum antibiotic resistance. Notably, approximately 12% of Escherichia coli isolates and 43% of Klebsiella species isolated from blood samples exhibited carbapenem resistance, underscoring the growing challenge posed by AMR in the state.8

Considering the increasing burden of antimicrobial resistance and the crucial role of healthcare professionals in combating its spread, it is essential that nursing students possess adequate knowledge and a positive attitude towards antimicrobial resistance and its prevention. Therefore, the present study was undertaken to assess the knowledge and attitudes regarding antimicrobial resistance and its effects among nursing students.

Need and significance of the study

An institution-based cross-sectional study conducted among 323 undergraduate paramedical students at the University of Gondar, Ethiopia, to assess knowledge and attitudes towards antimicrobial resistance reported that nearly 96% of participants perceived antimicrobial resistance as a serious yet preventable public health problem. However, approximately 55% of participants had limited knowledge of antimicrobial resistance. The study also demonstrated statistically significant differences in knowledge and attitudes across different departments (p < 0.0001 and p = 0.002, respectively). Furthermore, participants with good knowledge had significantly higher attitude scores than those with moderate or poor knowledge (p < 0.0001).9

A multi-center cross-sectional study involving 848 nursing students, nurses, and other healthcare professionals in Italy assessed knowledge, attitudes, and practices (KAP) regarding antimicrobial resistance. Among the participants, 61.9% (n = 525) were students and 37.3% (n = 316) were registered nurses. Most participants were female (71.6%), with a median age of 22 years, and 82.3% resided in southern Italy. Nearly 40% (39.6%) of participants demonstrated low KAP scores, highlighting substantial gaps in awareness and practices regarding to antimicrobial resistance.10

Similarly, a descriptive cross-sectional study conducted among 578 nursing students aged 18 years and above at the University of Santiago de Compostela, Spain, evaluated knowledge and awareness regarding antibiotic use, resistance, and stewardship. The study found that the students had a low level of knowledge about antibiotics, particularly concerning antibiotic resistance, with a mean score of 4.1 (95% CI: 3.4-4.8).11

These findings indicate that inadequate knowledge regarding antimicrobial resistance remains a global concern among nursing and allied health students. Since nurses play a pivotal role in the rational use of antibiotics, infection prevention, and patient education, strengthening their understanding of antimicrobial resistance is essential. Incorporating comprehensive training on antimicrobial stewardship, appropriate antibiotic use, and infection control measures into the nursing curriculum could contribute significantly to combating antimicrobial resistance. Therefore, the present study was undertaken to assess the knowledge and attitudes regarding antimicrobial resistance and its effects among nursing students, with the aim of identifying knowledge gaps and promoting appropriate educational interventions.

Objectives of the study

  1. Assess the knowledge regarding antimicrobial resistance and its effects among nursing students in a selected nursing college in Thiruvananthapuram.
  2. Assess the attitudes towards antimicrobial resistance and its effects among nursing students in a selected nursing college, Thiruvananthapuram.
  3. To determine the correlation between knowledge and attitude on antimicrobial resistance and its effects among nursing students in a selected nursing college in Thiruvananthapuram.
  4. To determine the association between knowledge regarding antimicrobial resistance and selected socio-personal variables such as age, gender, religion, area of residence, and previous knowledge regarding antimicrobial resistance.

Operational definition

Knowledge: refers to nursing students' awareness and understanding of antimicrobial resistance and its effects, as assessed using a structured questionnaire.

Attitude: refers to the tendency to respond positively or negatively towards antimicrobial resistance and its effects, as measured using a five-point Likert scale.

Antimicrobial resistance: refers to the ability of microorganisms to develop resistance to antimicrobial agents that are intended to eliminate them.

Nursing students: refers to 4th semester BSc Nursing students of KIMS College of Nursing, Thiruvananthapuram.

Assumptions

  • Nursing students may have limited knowledge and varying attitudes regarding antimicrobial resistance and its effects.
  • Educational interventions and awareness sessions may improve knowledge and attitudes towards antimicrobial resistance and its prevention.

Hypothesis

H1: There is a significant correlation between knowledge and attitudes regarding antimicrobial resistance and its effects among nursing students.

H2: There is a significant association between knowledge regarding antimicrobial resistance and selected socio-personal variables such as age, gender, religion, area of residence, and previous knowledge regarding antimicrobial resistance.

Data collection process

After obtaining ethical clearance from the Institutional Review Board and formal permission from the management of KIMS College of Nursing, Thiruvananthapuram, data were collected between June 19, 2025, and June 26, 2025. Participants who fulfilled the inclusion criteria were selected using a purposive sampling technique. The purpose of the study was explained to the participants using a participant information sheet, and written informed consent was obtained. A structured questionnaire was administered to assess knowledge and attitudes regarding antimicrobial resistance among the nursing students. Following completion of data collection, an awareness session on antimicrobial resistance was conducted, and an information booklet on antimicrobial resistance and its effects was provided to the participants.

Findings of the study

Section 1: Distribution of the sample according to socio-personal variables

  • Among the study participants, 77% were female, and 23% were male.
  • More than half of the participants (52%) were Hindus.
  • Most participants (75%) resided in urban areas, while 25% belonged to rural areas.

Sixty-two percent of participants had prior knowledge of antimicrobial resistance, whereas 38% had none.

Section 2: Distribution of the sample according to knowledge

  • Among the study participants, 55% had good knowledge regarding antimicrobial resistance and its effects, 32% had average knowledge, and 13% had poor knowledge.

Section 3: Distribution of the sample according to attitude

  • All study participants (100%) demonstrated a positive attitude towards antimicrobial resistance and its prevention.

Section 4: Correlation between knowledge and attitude on antimicrobial resistance and its effects among nursing students

The correlation coefficient revealed a weak positive correlation between knowledge and attitude scores (r = 0.170). However, the association was not statistically significant (p = 0.091), indicating that no significant relationship existed between knowledge and attitudes regarding antimicrobial resistance and its effects among nursing students.

Section 5: Association between knowledge on antimicrobial resistance and its effects with selected socio-personal variables

  • No statistically significant association was observed between knowledge scores and gender (χ2 = 2.750, p = 0.253), religion (χ2 = 1.915, p = 0.751), or area of residence (χ2 = 2.332, p = 0.312).
  • However, a statistically significant association was observed between knowledge scores and previous knowledge regarding antimicrobial resistance (χ2 = 70.366, p < 0.001).

Discussion

The present study was conducted to assess the knowledge and attitudes regarding antimicrobial resistance and its effects among nursing students. A descriptive research design was adopted, and participants were selected using a non-probability purposive sampling technique. The study was conducted among 100 fourth-semester BSc Nursing students at KIMS College of Nursing, Thiruvananthapuram, who met the inclusion criteria.

Conclusion

  • The present study assessed the knowledge and attitudes regarding antimicrobial resistance and its effects among nursing students. The findings indicate that most participants possessed good knowledge and demonstrated positive attitudes towards antimicrobial resistance and its prevention. Previous knowledge of antimicrobial resistance was significantly associated with knowledge scores, whereas no significant association was found with gender, religion, or area of residence. Furthermore, although a weak positive correlation was observed between knowledge and attitude scores, the relationship was not statistically significant.
  • The findings highlight the importance of continued educational initiatives and awareness programs to strengthen knowledge regarding antimicrobial resistance and promote the rational use of antimicrobial agents among future healthcare professionals.

articles.title: Cardiometabolic risk factors among airline and cargo pilots in Bahrain: A descriptive cross-sectional study

affiliations.text: Department of Family Medicine & Aviation Medicine, Royal Bahrain Hospital Medical Center, Janabiya, Bahrain.

abstract.heading: Background
abstract.text: Pilots are exposed to several occupational stressors, including long working schedules, circadian rhythm disturbances, sedentary work habits, and unhealthy lifestyle habits. These factors may increase the risk of cardiometabolic diseases. However, there is a paucity of information on the health status of pilots in the Middle East, particularly in Bahrain. A descriptive cross-sectional study was performed using medical and occupational data from active pilots in Bahrain.

abstract.heading: Objective
abstract.text: To characterise the prevalence of cardiometabolic risk factors and diseases among pilots in Bahrain and to examine their association with demographics, flight type, cumulative flight hours, and lifestyle habits.

abstract.heading: Methods
abstract.text: This descriptive cross-sectional study analyzed the medical and occupational records of pilots operating commercial passenger and cargo aircraft in Bahrain. Data collected included age, sex, nationality, flight hours, aircraft type, lifestyle behaviors (smoking and alcohol consumption), body mass index (BMI), and comorbidities such as hypertension, diabetes mellitus, dyslipidemia, and heart disease. Descriptive statistics and exploratory correlation analyses were performed. This was a descriptive cross-sectional observational study conducted among licensed airline and cargo pilots undergoing routine aeromedical examinations in Bahrain.

abstract.heading: Results
abstract.text: The sample population consisted predominantly of middle-aged men, most of whom were overweight or obese. A significant percentage of them had cardiometabolic risk factors, exceptionally high blood pressure, dyslipidemia, and diabetes. The prevalence of cardiometabolic conditions increased with higher cumulative flight hours, high BMI, and smoking.

abstract.heading: Conclusion
abstract.text: Cardiometabolic conditions are common among pilots in Bahrain and appear to be associated with occupational exposures and lifestyle factors. These findings highlight the need for targeted preventive strategies and health promotion measures within the field of aviation medicine.
