articles.bodyHtml:
Introduction

'Cardiometabolic disorders' refer to a cluster of metabolic abnormalities, including central obesity, dyslipidemia, insulin resistance, impaired glucose tolerance, and hypertension, collectively referred to as metabolic syndrome.1 Pilots are exposed to several occupational and lifestyle factors that may predispose them to these conditions. However, data on the cardiometabolic health of pilots in the Middle East are limited. This study aimed to characterize the prevalence of cardiometabolic risk factors and diseases among pilots in Bahrain and to examine their associations with demographic characteristics, type of flight operation, cumulative flight hours, and lifestyle habits.

Methods

This section describes the research design, population, data collection, and analytical methods used to investigate the cardiometabolic risk factors among pilots in Bahrain.

Study design

This cross-sectional study was based on data obtained from pilots undergoing initial aeromedical assessments and periodic medical revalidation examinations conducted by a certified Aviation Medical Examiner. Such a design enabled the assessment of the prevalence of cardiometabolic risk factors and diseases among the active flying population.2

Study population

The study population comprised licensed pilots operating commercial passenger and cargo aircraft in Bahrain who underwent routine aeromedical examinations during the study period.3 To reflect the multinational aviation workforce in the country, both Bahraini and non-Bahraini pilots were included. Pilots of both sexes were eligible, although the study population was predominantly male, consistent with the regional aviation workforce demographics.

Data analysis

Demographic, occupational, lifestyle, and clinical characteristics were summarized using descriptive statistics. Exploratory correlation analyses were performed to evaluate associations between cumulative flight hours, lifestyle behaviors, and cardiometabolic outcomes.

Results

Exploratory analyses revealed a higher burden of cardiometabolic risk factors among pilots with elevated BMI, longer cumulative flight hours, smoking habits, and those engaged in cargo flight operations.

Demographic and occupational characteristics

The study included 167 pilots employed in cargo aviation operations in Bahrain. The cohort consisted predominantly of men, with only a small proportion of women. Female pilots ranged in age from 27 to 45 years, whereas male pilots ranged in age from 27 to 64 years.

Occupational characteristics showed that the pilots operated a diverse range of aircraft, including Boeing 763, Boeing 737, Boeing 787, Airbus A320, Boeing 747, Avro, and Gulfstream 600, AURO RJ, and Gulfstream. Flight experience varied considerably across aircraft types and operators. Pilots flying commercial aircraft such as the Boeing 767 and Boeing 737 had accumulated more than 20,000 flight hours, whereas those operating smaller business jets, including Gulfstream aircraft, generally had fewer than 6,000 flight hours.

Comparison of airline and cargo pilots suggested differences in occupational exposures and lifestyle factors that may influence cardiometabolic risk. Combined use of alcohol and smoking were uncommon in both groups. Airline pilots had higher cumulative flight hours, ranging from 12,000-23,750 hours, and reported moderate levels of stress related to sleep disturbances. Differences in work environment and operational demands between large commercial aircraft and smaller aircraft may contribute to variations in occupational stress and cardiometabolic risk between the two groups.

Anthropometric and cardiometabolic profile

Overweight and obesity were common among the pilots, with BMI values ranging from normal to morbidly obese (≥35 kg/m2). Obesity was found to be more prevalent among airline pilots than cargo pilots, suggesting that differences in workload or lifestyle patterns may contribute to variations in BMI between these groups.4

Exploratory analyses indicated a greater burden of cardiometabolic conditions among pilots with higher cumulative flight hours. Lifestyle factors, including smoking, alcohol consumption, and severe obesity (BMI ≥ 35 kg/m2), were also associated with increased cardiometabolic risk. Hypertension, diabetes, dyslipidemia, and cardiovascular disease were more common among pilots with greater flight exposure and unhealthy lifestyle behaviors.

These findings are consistent with those reported by Andisi-Musambi et al. (2023), who observed a higher prevalence of smoking among men than women, with 33.4% of adult men reporting regular tobacco use. The influence of these lifestyle factors is reflected in the prevalence of hypertension (42.7%), hypercholesterolemia (40.2%), and diabetes mellitus (14.5%) in the general population.6

Conversely, pilots with lower cumulative flight hours and healthier lifestyle behaviors exhibited lower burden of cardiometabolic disorders. Smoking, particularly at higher levels (e.g., ≥10 cigarettes per day), appeared to further increase this risk, whereas moderate alcohol consumption alone had a relatively minor effect unless accompanied by other risk factors. Severe obesity (BMI ≥35 kg/m2) emerged as an important risk factor for adverse cardiometabolic outcomes.

These findings suggest that there is a cumulative influence of occupational exposures and lifestyle factors on cardiometabolic health, and underscore the need for having targeted preventive interventions within aviation medicine (Figure 2).

Lifestyle behaviors

The lifestyle habits among the pilots in this cohort were heterogeneous, with smoking and alcohol consumption being the key modifiable risk factors for cardiometabolic health.5 Traditional cigarette smoking (typically 10–15 cigarettes per day) was the most common form of tobacco use among male pilots, although some also reported the use of shisha and electronic cigarettes (e-cigarettes) or vaping devices. Among female pilots, e-cigarettes and vaping devices were more commonly used, while a smaller proportion reported conventional cigarette smoking. Some pilots described their smoking behavior as occasional or social.

Alcohol consumption was generally moderate, with most pilots reporting one or two drinks per occasion, whereas others reported that they abstained from alcohol or consumed it only occasionally. No cases of heavy or chronic alcohol use were identified. Combined exposure to smoking and alcohol consumption, a potentially more adverse cardiometabolic profile, was observed in only a small proportion of pilots.

Several occupational factors inherent to professional aviation, including shift work, irregular schedules, circadian rhythm disruption, sleep disturbances, prolonged sedentary behaviour, and psychological stress, may adversely affect cardiometabolic health.

Occupational, lifestyle, and cardiometabolic outcomes

Exploratory analyses were performed to investigate the relationships between occupational exposures, lifestyle behaviours, and cardiometabolic outcomes among pilots. Greater cumulative flight hours were associated with a higher burden of cardiometabolic conditions, including hypertension, diabetes mellitus, dyslipidaemia, and cardiovascular disease. Pilots with more than 15,000 cumulative flight hours appeared to have a greater prevalence of these conditions than those with fewer flight hours.

Another important correlate was body mass index (BMI). Overweight and obese pilots (BMI ≥ 25 kg/m2) exhibited higher prevalence of hypertension, dyslipidemia, and diabetes. Severe obesity (BMI ≥35 kg/m2) was associated with the highest burden of multimorbidity, suggesting a cumulative effect of cardiometabolic risk factors. This result aligns with previous reports showing the prevalence of hypertension was higher among men (13.8%) than women (2.8%), with prevalence increasing with advancing age.

Lifestyle behaviours also showed notable associations with cardiometabolic outcomes. Smoking and frequent alcohol consumption were associated with a greater burden of hypertension and dyslipidaemia. These conditions were more common among pilots who smoked at least 10 cigarettes per day and those who consumed alcohol frequently, compared with non-smokers and those with lower alcohol intake. Although vaping and occasional social smoking, which were more commonly reported by female pilots, appeared to be associated with a lower prevalence of cardiometabolic conditions, these behaviours remained potential risk factors, particularly when combined with elevated BMI and greater cumulative flight exposure.

There were also significant correlations between lifestyle behaviours and cardiometabolic outcomes. Smoking and frequent drinking were associated with a greater burden of hypertension and dyslipidaemia. Hypertension and dyslipidemia were more common among pilots who smoked at least 10 cigarettes per day and those who used alcohol frequently, compared with non-smokers who had lower alcohol intake. Vaping and occasional social smoking, which were more frequent in female pilots, were linked to a reduced incidence of cardiometabolic diseases, although they remained risk factors in combination with high BMI and greater cumulative flight exposure.

In Bahrain, approximately 10.8% of adults self-report diabetes mellitus, whereas the overall prevalence, including previously undiagnosed cases, is estimated to be around 15%. These findings highlight the importance of addressing both occupational and lifestyle factors to mitigate cardiometabolic risk among pilots.

Discussion

This study provides one of the first descriptive assessments of cardiometabolic health among a medically screened population of pilots in Bahrain. Despite compliance with stringent aeromedical fitness requirements, hypertension, diabetes mellitus, dyslipidaemia, and cardiovascular disease were common. These findings suggest that occupational exposures and lifestyle factors may contribute to cardiometabolic risk in this population.

Cumulative flight hours are one of the findings in this study because the cardiometabolic risk is associated with cumulative flight hours. The older pilots with more than 15,000 hours of flight experience were more likely to experience hypertension, diabetes, dyslipidemia, and heart disease.6

Body mass index (BMI) emerged as an important correlate of cardiometabolic risk. Hypertension, dyslipidemia, and diabetes were more prevalent in overweight and obese pilots (BMI ≥ 25 kg/m2), whereas multiple comorbidities were more prevalent among those with severe obesity (BMI ≥ 35 kg/m2). These observations support the notion that prolonged sedentary work, irregular schedules, and limited opportunities for structured physical activity may contribute to weight gain and adverse metabolic outcomes.7 Obesity may also amplify the effects of other risk factors, including smoking and unhealthy dietary habits.

It was observed that lifestyle behaviors have a significant effect on cardiometabolic health. Conventional cigarette smoking, shisha use, and electronic cigarette use were reported among the cohort, with conventional cigarette smoking being more common among male pilots and vaping more frequently reported by female pilots. Smoking is a well-established risk factor for hypertension, atherosclerosis, insulin resistance, and dyslipidaemia. Alcohol consumption was generally moderate, with most pilots reporting one to two drinks per occasion and only a small proportion reporting infrequent social drinking. Although electronic cigarettes and vaping devices may expose users to fewer toxic substances than conventional cigarettes, they remain potential contributors to adverse metabolic and cardiovascular effects, particularly when combined with elevated BMI and prolonged occupational exposure.6

Occupational characteristics appeared to influence cardiometabolic risk. Pilots with greater cumulative flight hours had a higher burden of hypertension, diabetes mellitus, dyslipidaemia, and cardiovascular disease. In particular, pilots with more than 15,000 cumulative flight hours exhibited a greater prevalence of these conditions. Although pilots in this cohort reported lower rates of smoking and alcohol use than the general adult population in Bahrain, they demonstrated substantial burdens of cardiometabolic disease, suggesting that prolonged flight exposure, circadian disruption, irregular work schedules, psychological stress, and sedentary work may contribute to adverse health outcomes.

Comparatively, pilots in this study had lower rates of smoking and alcohol use than the general adult population in Bahrain, yet they exhibited higher prevalence of hypertension, diabetes, and dyslipidemia. The findings support a cumulative risk model, in which occupational exposures interact with lifestyle factors and individual characteristics to influence cardiometabolic health. High BMI, smoking, and prolonged flight exposure appeared to exert additive effects on the prevalence of hypertension, dyslipidaemia, diabetes mellitus, and cardiovascular disease. The findings underscore the need for targeted health interventions and monitoring specific to the aviation profession.8

Regional and cultural factors should also be considered. The use of alternative tobacco products, including shisha and electronic cigarettes, reflects local social practices and highlights the need for culturally sensitive health promotion programmes. Preventive strategies tailored to the aviation profession should address smoking cessation, weight management, physical activity, sleep hygiene, and regular cardiometabolic screening.

Overall, this study demonstrates that cardiometabolic disorders are common among pilots in Bahrain and that cumulative flight hours, obesity, smoking, alcohol consumption, and occupational factors may collectively contribute to cardiometabolic risk.

Strengths and limitations

The study benefits from a heterogeneous and sizeable pilot cohort, representing multiple nationalities, flight types, and experience levels.

Strengths

This study has several strengths. It included a relatively large and heterogeneous cohort of 167 pilots representing different nationalities, age groups, experience levels, and both airline and cargo operations, thereby providing a broad overview of cardiometabolic health among pilots in Bahrain. The use of routinely collected aeromedical examination data from an active flying population enhances the clinical relevance of the findings and offers valuable insights into occupational and lifestyle factors associated with cardiometabolic risk in a medically screened workforce.

Limitations

This study has several limitations. First, its cross-sectional design precludes establishing causal or temporal relationships between occupational exposures, lifestyle behaviors, and cardiometabolic outcomes.8 Second, the use of routinely documented medical information may have resulted in underrecognition of subclinical or undiagnosed cardiometabolic diseases, since pilots are assessed periodically, and mostly only clinically manifested disease is reported. Third, smoking, alcohol consumption, and vaping behaviors were partly self-reported, introducing the possibility of reporting bias and misclassification.

Conclusion

This study provides a broad review of cardiometabolic health among pilots in Bahrain. Despite routine aeromedical screening, hypertension, diabetes mellitus, dyslipidaemia, and cardiovascular disease were common. Greater cumulative flight hours, elevated BMI, smoking, alcohol consumption, and occupational exposures appeared to contribute to increased cardiometabolic risk. These findings underscore the need for targeted preventive strategies and regular cardiometabolic surveillance within aviation medicine.

Implications for practice

The adoption of the following evidence-based measures would allow for mitigating cardiometabolic risk, improving the well-being of pilots, and enabling safe and sustainable operations in the aviation industry:

  1. Incorporate periodic cardiometabolic risk assessment in addition to age-based aeromedical evaluations.
  2. Develop aviation-specific smoking cessation programs addressing conventional cigarettes, shisha, and electronic cigarettes.
  3. Promote structured weight management and physical activity programmes.
  4. Encourage interventions aimed at improving sleep hygiene and mitigating circadian disruption.
  5. Establish preventive health programs tailored to airline and cargo pilots.

abstract.text: Knee osteoarthritis (KOA) is one of the most prevalent musculoskeletal disorders worldwide, affecting over 250 million individuals and imposing a substantial socioeconomic burden. Intra-articular hyaluronic acid (HA) and platelet-rich plasma (PRP) injections have emerged as the two leading non-surgical biologic therapies. Over the past 20 years, numerous randomized controlled trials (RCTs), systematic reviews, and meta-analyses have evaluated the comparative efficacy and safety of these modalities. This review synthesizes evidence published between 2005 and 2025, comparing HA and PRP injections with respect to pain relief, functional outcomes, durability of therapeutic benefit, safety profiles, and cost considerations.

articles.bodyHtml:
Introduction

Knee osteoarthritis (KOA) is a degenerative joint disease characterized by progressive cartilage loss, subchondral bone remodeling, synovial inflammation, and osteophyte formation resulting in pain, functional limitation, and reduced mobility. It affects approximately 16% of the global population aged 15 years or older and 22.9% of those aged 40 years or older, with prevalence increasing substantially with advancing age and being higher among women. According to a recent (2023) systematic review, the prevalence of osteoarthritis in Saudi Arabia is between 13% and 41%. KOA is considered one of the leading causes of disability in older adults.1–3 Management is to be done in steps. The initial approach is to be conservative, and the treatment includes lifestyle modifications, physiotherapy, and oral analgesics. When these measures fail to provide adequate relief, intra-articular injections or surgical intervention may be indicated.4

Hyaluronic acid (HA) visco-supplementation was introduced in the 1990s and gained widespread clinical acceptance in the early 2000s. HA is a naturally occurring glycosaminoglycan present in synovial fluid that contributes to joint lubrication and shock absorption. In osteoarthritic joints, both the concentration and molecular weight of endogenous HA are reduced, contributing to pain and stiffness. Exogenous HA injections aim to restore the viscoelastic properties of synovial fluid, reduce friction, and modulate inflammation.5

Platelet-rich plasma (PRP) emerged in orthopedic practice in the mid-2000s. PRP is an autologous blood product containing supraphysiologic concentrations of platelets and growth factors, including transforming growth factor-β (TGF-β), platelet-derived growth factor (PDGF), vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF), and insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1). These bioactive molecules promote tissue repair, modulate inflammation, stimulate endogenous HA synthesis, and recruit mesenchymal stem cells.6,7 Compared to HA, PRP is believed to provide long-term clinical benefits (Table 1). Despite the widespread use of both therapies, considerable debate persists regarding their relative efficacy, optimal preparation protocols, injection schedules, and patient selection criteria. This review aims to provide a comprehensive comparison of HA and PRP based on the cumulative evidence generated over the past two decades.

Discussion

Pain relief

The Visual Analog Scale (VAS) and the Western Ontario and McMaster Universities Osteoarthritis Index (WOMAC) pain subscale are validated patient-reported outcome measures widely used to assess pain severity and treatment effectiveness in patients with KOA, with lower scores indicating greater pain relief. Across most major meta-analyses published to date, PRP has demonstrated superior pain reduction compared to HA, when measured by the VAS and WOMAC pain subscale. Belk et al. (2021), analyzing 18 level-1 studies, reported that 6 of 11 VAS-based studies showed significantly lower pain in PRP patients at the latest follow-up (p < 0.05). Furthermore, the mean improvement in the WOMAC pain subscale was 44.7% with PRP compared with 12.6% with HA (p < 0.01).8 The most recent and largest meta-analysis by Li et al. (2025), encompassing 42 randomized controlled trials, confirmed PRP's superiority over HA in reducing VAS pain at 3, 6, and 12 months after injection.9

Functional outcomes

Functional improvement in terms of knee symptoms, physical function, and the ability to perform daily and sports-related activities is measured most commonly by the WOMAC total score and the International Knee Documentation Committee (IKDC) score. Similar to pain outcomes, functional outcome measures generally favor PRP over HA. Han et al. (2019) found significantly better WOMAC function scores in the PRP group at 3, 6, and 12 months.10 A retrospective cohort study by Al-Sharif et al. (2025) comparing PRP, HA, corticosteroids, and NSAIDs in 205 patients demonstrated mean WOMAC scores of 46 ± 9 for PRP and 48 ± 10 for HA at 10–12 months, a narrower gap than in some meta-analyses, but PRP still showed the most sustained improvement.11

Durability

One of the most clinically significant advantages of PRP is its longer-lasting effect. HA injections typically provide symptom relief lasting 3–6 months and often require repeat courses every 6 months, with possibly diminishing efficacy. In contrast, PRP outcomes frequently demonstrate sustained improvement for 12 months or longer. The durability is attributed to PRP's biological disease-modifying properties, growth factor–mediated chondrocyte repair, and endogenous HA synthesis rather than HA's purely mechanical visco supplementation.8,12

Influence of PRP composition

Not all PRP preparations are equal. A critical distinction exists between leukocyte-poor PRP (LP-PRP) and leukocyte-rich PRP (LR-PRP). Belk et al. (2021) found that LP-PRP was associated with significantly better IKDC scores than LR-PRP (p < 0.05).8 The catabolic enzymes and pro-inflammatory cytokines released by white blood cells in LR-PRP may partially counteract the beneficial effects of platelet-derived growth factors. This heterogeneity in PRP preparation remains one of the most important confounders across studies and underscores the need for standardized classification systems, such as the Platelets, Activation, White blood cells (PAW) classification.

Effect of disease severity

Both PRP and HA therapies are more effective in patients with early-to-moderate KOA, corresponding to Kellgren-Lawrence grades I–III. Al-Sharif et al. (2025) showed that patients with KL grade II disease experienced significantly greater VAS improvement than those with KL grade III (3.8 ± 0.9 vs. 2.6 ± 1.1, p = 0.019) disease in the PRP group and the HA group (3.5 vs. 2.7, p = 0.026).11 In advanced disease (KL grade IV), neither injection modality provides reliable benefit, and surgical options should be considered.

Combination therapy (PRP and HA)

Emerging evidence suggests that combining PRP and HA may provide synergistic benefits. A 2024 meta-analysis of 11 randomised control trials (RCT) (n = 1,023) found that the combination therapy produced superior long-term VAS scores (MD −4.27, 95% CI: −4.96 to −3.58; p < 0.001) and WOMAC scores (MD −1.77, 95% CI: −2.20 to −1.34; p < 0.001) compared with PRP alone, with a lower incidence of adverse events (RR 0.41, 95% CI: 0.35–0.48).11 Chen et al. (2021) similarly demonstrated that combined HA and PRP achieved better VAS pain reduction than PRP alone at 6 months (p = 0.020) in KL grade II patients.13

Safety profile

Both HA and PRP carry favorable safety profiles. The most common adverse events include transient injection-site pain, mild swelling, and stiffness, which are self-limiting. Li et al. (2025) noted a slightly higher incidence of mild adverse events in the PRP group, but no serious complications were reported in either arm across 42 RCTs.9 HA carries a small risk of pseudo-septic reactions (acute flare), estimated at 1–2%, particularly with high-molecular-weight preparations. PRP, being autologous, has a negligible risk of allergic or immune-mediated reactions.

Quality of evidence: A cautionary note

Despite the growing body of evidence favoring PRP, the quality of the evidence base warrants caution. In an umbrella review of 17 systematic reviews, Chen et al. (2024) evaluated the methodology using the A MeaSurement Tool to Assess Systematic Reviews 2 (AMSTAR-2), Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA 2020) and Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) systems. They found that all 17 reviews were rated "extremely low" in methodological quality, with substantial overlap among the primary studies.14 These findings underscore the need for large, multi-center, well-designed RCTs with standardized PRP preparation protocols, adequate blinding, and long-term follow-up extending beyond 24 months.

The comparative evidence base has evolved considerably over the past two decades, progressing from small single-center randomized trials conducted between 2005 and 2012 to larger and more methodologically robust systematic reviews and meta-analyses published thereafter (Table 2).

Conclusions

The cumulative evidence of the past two decades supports the following conclusions:

  1. Platelet-rich plasma (PRP) is associated with greater pain relief and functional improvement than hyaluronic acid (HA), with benefits persisting at 3, 6, and 12 months in most studies.
  2. PRP offers longer-lasting benefits, reducing the frequency of repeat injections.
  3. Leukocyte-poor PRP appears to outperform leukocyte-rich formulations and should be preferred when available.
  4. HA remains a reasonable and accessible option, particularly for patients in whom PRP is cost-prohibitive or unavailable, and for those seeking rapid onset of relief.
  5. Combination PRP and HA therapy is a promising frontier with emerging evidence of synergistic benefit.
  6. Both therapies are most effective in early-to-moderate disease (KL grades I–III).
  7. The overall evidence quality remains low, and future research must prioritize standardized PRP preparation, double-blinded study designs, and follow-up beyond 24 months.
  8. Clinicians should adopt a personalized, shared-decision approach, weighing disease severity, patient age and activity level, cost constraints, and local availability when choosing between HA and PRP for knee osteoarthritis management.

abstract.text: Intraoperative ultrasound (IOUS) is a real-time imaging modality with considerable potential to improve the safety and outcomes of neurosurgical procedures. It provides real-time image guidance and is radiation-free, repeatable, readily available, easily integrated into the existing operating room workflow, and more cost-effective than other intraoperative imaging modalities such as intraoperative magnetic resonance imaging (iMRI) and intraoperative computed tomography (iCT). The clinical applications of IOUS are broad and include brain and spinal tumors, intracranial hematomas, stereotactic biopsies, and catheter guidance. In this article, we briefly describe the various applications of IOUS and share our experience with its use at our center.

articles.bodyHtml:
Introduction

Intraoperative imaging technologies continue to evolve and have become integral to modern neurosurgical practice. Reliable intraoperative orientation is one of the most important determinants of safe and effective neurosurgery.1 Image-guided modalities such as frame-based and frameless neuronavigation, intraoperative ultrasound (IOUS), intraoperative computed tomography (iCT), and intraoperative magnetic resonance imaging (iMRI) enable neurosurgeons to accurately localize lesions and adjacent structures, facilitate surgical planning, and achieve safe maximal resection.

Neuronavigation is affected by brain shift that occurs once surgery begins, mainly due to cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) drainage, and therefore does not provide real-time navigation.2 The other three modalities—IOUS, intraoperative CT (iCT), and intraoperative MRI (iMRI)—provide real-time imaging and accurate information during surgery.3 Although intraoperative CT and MRI are more advanced imaging modalities, they are expensive and require infrastructure and logistics that are not feasible in most operating room settings.

IOUS, on the other hand, can be easily integrated into the existing operating room workflow. Recent advances in technology have significantly improved the image quality of IOUS.

In this article, we share how IOUS helps in various neurosurgical procedures and describe our experience with its use at our center.

Gadgets

We initially used Sonosite probes, which had large footprints. Over the last year, we acquired the BK5000 neurosurgical transducers, which are specialized, high-resolution, sterilizable transducers designed specifically for neurosurgical applications. Disposable, easy-to-use needle guides assist in accurate targeting of lesions.

Figures 1a and 1b show the transducers.

The spectrum of applications includes intracranial hemorrhages, brain tumors, colloid cysts, brain biopsies, guidance for ventriculoperitoneal (VP) shunt placement, and determining the optimal site for myelotomy in spinal tumors.4

Illustrative case 1

An elderly patient presented with a right frontal ICSOL.

A craniotomy with IOUS was performed. After opening the dura, the BK transducer was used to localize the tumor (Figure 4b).

After the initial resection, the resection cavity was filled with saline, and IOUS was used again to look for any residual lesion (Figure 4c).

This provided real-time navigation, and the residual lesion was subsequently resected (Figure 4d).

Case 2

A young female patient with a colloid cyst and hydrocephalus.

Case 3

A small lesion in the cingulate gyrus.

Conclusion

IOUS clearly defines tumor margins and facilitates safe tumor resection. It improves the extent of resection of intraparenchymal brain tumors. Furthermore, early tumor-bed hematomas can be recognized, as they have a characteristic appearance on ultrasound. It does not require any changes in patient positioning or the intraoperative setting, while at the same time offering excellent spatial and temporal resolution. Real-time intraoperative imaging technologies have shown utility in assisting tumor resection in a dynamic surgical field.5 Increasing attention has been paid to IOUS, which has been reported to be a widely accessible, portable, space-saving, and reliable imaging modality that enables surgeons to follow and modify the surgical plan in real time.

articles.title: Unmasking the unusual: Atypical manifestations of gastric carcinoma and their diagnostic challenges

affiliations.text: Department of Gastroenterology, KIMSHEALTH, Trivandrum, Kerala, India.

abstract.text: Gastric carcinoma is a major contributor to cancer-related morbidity and mortality worldwide and typically presents with upper gastrointestinal symptoms or metastases involving the liver, peritoneum, lungs, and lymph nodes. However, uncommon metastatic sites and rare histological variants may obscure the diagnosis and delay appropriate management. We report three unusual presentations of gastric carcinoma encountered at a tertiary care center. The first case involved a 57-year-old woman who presented with isolated left wrist pain and was found to have a solitary lytic lesion of the triquetrum. Histopathological examination and immunohistochemistry of the lesion confirmed metastatic adenocarcinoma, leading to the diagnosis of gastric cardia adenocarcinoma with acrometastasis. The second case was a 36-year-old woman presenting with orbital apex syndrome characterized by headache, ptosis, diplopia, and visual impairment. Subsequent evaluation revealed diffuse gastric wall involvement, and gastric biopsy demonstrated poorly cohesive adenocarcinoma with signet ring cells, establishing the diagnosis of orbital metastasis from gastric carcinoma. The third case involved a 50-year-old man presenting with jaundice, multiple liver lesions, and markedly elevated serum alpha-fetoprotein levels, initially raising suspicion of hepatocellular carcinoma. Histopathological and immunohistochemical evaluation ultimately revealed hepatoid adenocarcinoma of gastric origin with liver metastases. These cases highlight the diverse clinical spectrum of gastric carcinoma and emphasize the importance of maintaining a high index of suspicion when evaluating atypical skeletal, orbital, or hepatic lesions. Careful correlation of clinical, radiological, histopathological, and immunohistochemical findings remains crucial for accurate diagnosis, particularly when gastric carcinoma presents in an unusual manner outside the gastrointestinal tract.

articles.bodyHtml:
Introduction

Gastric carcinoma remains one of the most common malignancies worldwide and is a leading cause of cancer-related mortality, particularly in Asia. Despite a declining global incidence, it continues to pose a significant healthcare burden because many patients present with advanced disease at the time of diagnosis. Histologically, gastric adenocarcinoma is broadly classified into intestinal and diffuse types, each exhibiting distinct biological behavior and patterns of spread.

Patients typically present with nonspecific symptoms such as dyspepsia, early satiety, epigastric pain, anorexia, weight loss, anemia, or upper gastrointestinal bleeding. The most common sites of metastasis include the liver, peritoneum, distant lymph nodes, lungs, and bones.1 However, gastric carcinoma can occasionally manifest through unusual metastatic sites or rare histological variants, posing considerable diagnostic challenges and often delaying definitive diagnosis.

Rare metastatic manifestations may occasionally precede gastrointestinal symptoms, thereby creating diagnostic dilemmas.2 We describe three unusual presentations of gastric carcinoma diagnosed through distinctive histopathological and immunohistochemical findings.

Case series

Case 1: Gastric adenocarcinoma presenting as triquetral acrometastasis

A 57-year-old woman presented with isolated left wrist pain of two months' duration. Imaging revealed an expansile lytic lesion involving the triquetrum. Fine-needle aspiration cytology (FNAC) from the extensor carpi ulnaris tendon suggested a poorly differentiated malignant neoplasm. PET-CT demonstrated metabolically active thickening of the gastric cardia extending to the gastroesophageal junction with a solitary fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG)-avid lytic lesion in the left triquetrum. Gastric biopsy revealed well-differentiated adenocarcinoma. Curettage of the wrist lesion showed lamellar bone infiltrated by malignant glands. Immunohistochemistry demonstrated positivity for CK7 and CK19, confirming metastatic adenocarcinoma consistent with a gastric primary. The final diagnosis was gastric adenocarcinoma with isolated triquetral acrometastasis.

Case 2: Orbital apex syndrome as the initial manifestation of signet-ring cell gastric carcinoma

A 36-year-old woman presented with headache, right-sided ptosis, diplopia, and visual impairment. Clinical examination revealed cranial nerve II, III, IV, and VI palsies consistent with orbital apex syndrome. Endoscopic transnasal biopsy of a right orbital apex mass showed a poorly differentiated malignant neoplasm. PET-CT evaluation subsequently identified diffuse gastric wall involvement suggestive of linitis plastica. Histopathological examination of gastric biopsies demonstrated a poorly cohesive carcinoma with signet-ring cell morphology. Correlation of the orbital lesion pathology with the gastric biopsy established the diagnosis of orbital metastasis from diffuse-type gastric adenocarcinoma, an exceptionally rare metastatic presentation.

Case 3: AFP-producing hepatoid gastric adenocarcinoma

A 50-year-old man with type 2 diabetes mellitus presented with jaundice, anorexia, weight loss, and multiple liver lesions. Laboratory evaluation revealed markedly elevated serum AFP levels exceeding 100,000 ng/mL, raising suspicion of hepatocellular carcinoma. Upper GI endoscopy was performed to look for varices, but showed an ulceroproliferative lesion along the lesser curvature of the stomach. Endoscopic biopsy of the gastric antral lesion showed poorly differentiated adenocarcinoma. Immunohistochemistry demonstrated BerEP4 positivity, focal Glypican-3 positivity, weak patchy AFP expression, and negativity for CK7 and CK20. These findings supported a diagnosis of gastric adenocarcinoma with hepatoid differentiation (hepatoid adenocarcinoma). The final diagnosis was hepatoid gastric adenocarcinoma with liver metastases.

Discussion

The most common sites of metastasis from gastric carcinoma are the liver, peritoneum, distant lymph nodes, lung, and bone.2

Acrometastasis accounts for only 0.1% of all osseous metastases and usually indicates an advanced primary malignancy.4 Although acrometastasis typically occurs in patients with a known primary malignancy, up to 10% of cases may present as the first clinical manifestation of an occult primary tumor. Gastrointestinal primaries account for only 3-15% of cases of bony metastases. The common sites of acrometastasis are distal phalanges (68.4%), carpal bones (14.2%), and metacarpals (14.2%), followed by other sites (3.2%).5 The most frequent primary tumors associated with acrometastases arise from the lung, breast, kidney, colon, rectum, prostate, and liver.

Orbital metastases from gastric carcinoma are exceedingly rare, comprising less than 0.1% of gastric cancer metastases and 2-7% of all orbital tumors.6 The most common primary tumors metastasizing to the orbit originate from the breast, lung, prostate, and kidney. The median survival following the diagnosis of orbital metastasis ranges from 3 to 8 months.

Hepatoid adenocarcinoma of the stomach (HAS) is a rare and highly aggressive subtype of gastric cancer, accounting for approximately 0.17–15% of gastric malignancies.8 It often presents at an advanced stage and lacks specific clinical features, making early diagnosis difficult. Histologically and immunophenotypically, HAS resembles hepatocellular carcinoma, which can further complicate diagnosis.9 Compared with conventional gastric adenocarcinoma, HAS demonstrates more aggressive behavior, a higher tendency for metastasis, and a poorer prognosis.10 Owing to its rarity, there is currently no standardized treatment approach, and management is largely based on available evidence and individual patient characteristics.

These cases highlight the remarkable heterogeneity of gastric cancer and underscore the importance of histopathological examination and immunohistochemistry in establishing the diagnosis when presentations are atypical.

Conclusion

Gastric carcinoma may initially manifest through rare metastatic sites or uncommon histological variants, often in the absence of significant gastrointestinal symptoms. Recognition of these atypical clinical presentations, along with judicious use of histopathology and immunohistochemistry, is essential for accurate diagnosis and timely management.

articles.title: An underrecognized toxicological emergency: Ciguatera fish poisoning presenting to a South Indian emergency department

affiliations.text: Department of Emergency Medicine, KIMSHEALTH, Trivandrum, Kerala, India.

abstract.heading: Background
abstract.text: Ciguatera fish poisoning (CFP) is an under-recognized marine toxin-mediated illness caused by the ingestion of reef fish contaminated with ciguatoxins. Although CFP is well documented in the Caribbean and Pacific regions, reports from India are scarce. Emergency physicians should be aware of its diverse gastrointestinal, neurological, and cardiovascular manifestations, particularly in coastal populations. This case series highlights the clinical spectrum and challenges associated with CFP in the Indian setting.

abstract.heading: Methods
abstract.text: This case series includes five patients who presented to the emergency department of KIMSHEALTH, Trivandrum, Kerala, with suspected ciguatera poisoning three to 24 hours after consuming fish, over a one-month period.

abstract.heading: Results
abstract.text: All patients presented with acute gastrointestinal symptoms, including vomiting, loose stools, and abdominal discomfort, within three to 24 hours of consuming reef fish. Three patients developed characteristic neurological symptoms, including paraesthesia and ataxia. Two patients exhibited cardiovascular features such as bradycardia and hypotension, requiring medical intervention. All cases were diagnosed clinically and supportive management resulted in favourable outcomes.

abstract.heading: Conclusion
abstract.text: Ciguatera fish poisoning should be considered in patients presenting with acute gastroenteritis and neurocardiological symptoms following reef fish consumption. Early recognition in the emergency department (ED) can prevent unnecessary investigations and ensure appropriate supportive care.

articles.bodyHtml:
Introduction

Ciguatera fish poisoning (CFP) is the most common non-bacterial seafood-borne illness worldwide and results from consumption of reef fish contaminated with heat-stable ciguatoxins produced by dinoflagellates such as Gambierdiscus toxicus. The toxin progressively bioaccumulates along the marine food chain and reaches its highest concentration in large predatory reef fish.

CFP is frequently underdiagnosed in emergency settings because of its protean clinical manifestations. Patients typically present with a combination of gastrointestinal, neurological, and cardiovascular symptoms. In India, particularly in coastal regions such as Kerala, sporadic cases occur but remain under-reported.

This case series describes five patients who presented to the ED with CFP, highlighting characteristic clinical patterns and management challenges.

Methods

This retrospective case series was conducted in the Emergency Department of KIMSHEALTH, Trivandrum, Kerala, over a one-month period from February to March 2026.

Inclusion criteria:

  • Recent history of reef fish consumption
  • Acute onset gastrointestinal symptoms
  • Associated neurological and/or cardiovascular symptoms

Data collected included patient demographics, time from symptom onset to presentation, clinical features, treatment provided, and clinical outcomes.

Case series

Case 1

A 55-year-old man presented with chest tightness, dizziness, and craniofacial paresthesia 24 hours after consuming reef fish. The patient reported that family members who shared the same meal experienced similar symptoms. He also had nausea, gastric discomfort, and diarrhoea. On initial evaluation, the patient exhibited hypotension and transient bradycardia, which subsequently progressed to a nadir heart rate of 21 bpm associated with worsening chest discomfort. Management included fluid resuscitation, vasopressor support with noradrenaline, and two doses of intravenous atropine (1 mg each). Following ICU admission and stabilization, the patient's symptoms resolved within 24 hours, and he was discharged in stable condition on the fourth hospital day.

Case 2

A 45-year-old woman presented with vomiting, loose stools, and vertigo three hours after consuming home-prepared fish. Her symptoms were subsequently complicated by bilateral upper limb paresthesia. Initial assessment at a primary healthcare facility revealed significant hypotension and bradycardia, for which she received 1 mg of atropine. Upon transfer to the Emergency Department, the patient received further fluid resuscitation and atropine before being admitted to the ICU for close hemodynamic monitoring. Her clinical course was uneventful. The patient remained asymptomatic during subsequent Holter monitoring and was discharged on the fourth hospital day.

Case 3

A 39-year-old male presented with generalized malaise, gastric bloating, loose stools, and ataxia 12 hours after consuming reef fish. He subsequently developed vertigo and emesis. On the second day of hospitalization, the patient experienced a rapid clinical deterioration characterized by acute ascending motor weakness, obtundation, and respiratory failure culminating in cardiopulmonary arrest. Return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) was achieved after one cycle of advanced cardiac life support (ACLS). The patient was subsequently maintained on inotropic and ventilatory support. Nerve conduction studies revealed motor polyneuropathy. The cerebrospinal fluid profile was normal. The patient was extubated on the fourth hospital day and achieved full clinical recovery by discharge on the seventh hospital day.

Case 4

A 51-year-old male presented with vomiting, perioral paresthesia, and gait instability three to four hours after consuming seafood. He reported a similar presentation in another person who had the same meal. The patient was admitted for neurological observation. Lumbar puncture was unremarkable. However, nerve conduction studies demonstrated evidence of demyelinating polyneuropathy in the upper extremities. In the absence of progressive motor deficits or features suggestive of Guillain-Barré syndrome, targeted therapy for it was deferred. The patient's symptoms resolved spontaneously, and he was discharged on hospital day 2.

Case 5

A 28-year-old man presented with abdominal pain, loose stools, perioral dysesthesia, and an oral burning sensation nine hours after consuming reef fish the previous evening. He later developed dizziness and ataxia. Clinical examination revealed mild bradycardia, though the patient remained hemodynamically stable without any evidence of gastrointestinal distress. Similar symptoms were reported by a co-diner, suggesting a common-source toxin exposure. The patient was managed conservatively with supportive care and had complete resolution of all neurological symptoms. He was discharged in stable condition on the third hospital day.

Results

The case series included five patients with a mean age of 43.6 years, with a male predominance (male: female ratio 4:1). All patients presented with prominent gastrointestinal symptoms, with vomiting and diarrhoea observed in all five cases (100%). Neurological manifestations were also similar, with paresthesia reported in all patients (100%), while ataxia was noted in two patients (40%). Cardiovascular involvement was observed in two patients, both of whom developed bradycardia and hypotension. The diagnosis of ciguatera poisoning was established clinically, based on the characteristic combination of gastrointestinal, neurological, and cardiovascular features along with a suggestive history of reef fish exposure. Two patients required pharmacologic intervention for cardiovascular instability. All patients recovered with supportive management and achieved complete clinical recovery.

Discussion

Ciguatera food poisoning is one of the most common marine toxin–related foodborne illnesses worldwide and results from ingestion of ciguatoxins that accumulate within the marine food chain. These toxins are produced by dinoflagellates of the genus Gambierdiscus and become concentrated in larger predatory reef fish through biomagnification.1

The disease occurs predominantly in tropical and subtropical regions, particularly in the Caribbean, Pacific islands, and parts of the Indian Ocean, with an estimated 50,000 cases occurring annually worldwide.2

The pathophysiology involves activation of voltage-gated sodium channels in neuronal and muscle cell membranes, resulting in persistent depolarization and increased neuronal excitability. Clinically, CFP typically follows a biphasic pattern with early gastrointestinal symptoms such as nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, and diarrhoea appearing within six to 24 hours after ingestion of contaminated fish. These gastrointestinal manifestations are frequently followed by neurological symptoms, including paresthesia, circumoral numbness, pruritus, myalgia, and dizziness.3

A distinctive clinical feature of CFP is paradoxical temperature perception (hot–cold reversal), in which cold stimuli are perceived as hot or painful, a symptom considered highly suggestive of the diagnosis. Cardiovascular manifestations such as bradycardia and hypotension may also occur, particularly in the acute phase of toxicity.4

Diagnosis of CFP remains largely clinical because no widely available laboratory test exists for confirming ciguatoxin exposure in humans. A detailed exposure history, particularly recent consumption of reef fish in association with compatible gastrointestinal and neurological symptoms, is therefore essential for establishing the diagnosis. Some patients may develop prolonged neurological symptoms such as dysesthesia, paresthesia, fatigue, or pruritus that can persist for weeks to months after the initial exposure. Recurrence or worsening of symptoms following alcohol consumption, caffeine intake, or consumption of certain foods has also been reported, possibly due to toxin redistribution.5

Management is primarily supportive and includes intravenous fluids, antiemetics, analgesia, and monitoring for cardiovascular complications. Intravenous mannitol (0.5–1 g/kg) has been proposed as a treatment for severe neurological manifestations; however, evidence for its effectiveness remains inconsistent.6

In Thiruvananthapuram, Kerala, CFP has been reported only sporadically, suggesting that the condition is uncommon but likely under-recognized. A suspected outbreak reported from Thiruvananthapuram in 2016 involved six individuals who developed symptoms after consuming cooked red snapper (Lutjanus bohar) purchased from a local market. Five of the affected individuals belonged to the same family. Symptoms developed approximately six hours after ingestion, and included vomiting, diarrhoea, circumoral paraesthesia, and paraesthesia of the upper and lower limbs. One patient exhibited the characteristic paradoxical temperature reversal, while another developed sinus bradycardia. Most patients remained haemodynamically stable. Symptoms persisted for one to four days in most cases, although prolonged neurological symptoms lasting several months were reported in one individual. This outbreak highlights the likelihood that CFP may be underdiagnosed in the region because of limited awareness and lack of confirmatory toxin testing.7

Our case series highlights the importance of obtaining a detailed dietary history in patients presenting with unexplained gastrointestinal symptoms followed by neurological and cardiological complaints. Recognition of this characteristic symptom constellation can facilitate timely diagnosis, avoid unnecessary investigations, and guide appropriate supportive management.

Limitations

This study has several limitations.

First, the small sample size limits the generalizability of our findings. Although the cases highlight important clinical patterns of ciguatoxin poisoning, the number of patients included is insufficient to draw definitive conclusions regarding the full spectrum of clinical manifestations, treatment responses, or outcomes. Larger multicenter studies are required to better characterize the epidemiology and clinical variability of the condition.

Second, laboratory confirmation of ciguatoxin exposure was unavailable, and the diagnosis was primarily based on clinical features and a suggestive dietary history. Although this reflects routine clinical practice, the absence of toxin assays introduces the possibility of misclassification with other seafood-related toxic syndromes.

Third, this was a single center study, which may limit the external validity of the findings. The observed clinical patterns may be influenced by regional dietary habits, locally consumed fish species, and people's healthcare-seeking behaviour, and therefore may not be fully representative of other populations.

Finally, the retrospective nature of data collection may have led to incomplete documentation of certain symptoms, timelines, or exposure history. Prospective studies with standardized data collection and confirmatory toxin analysis are needed to provide stronger evidence regarding the clinical features and optimal management of CFP.

Conclusion

Ciguatera fish poisoning, though uncommon, should be considered in patients presenting to the emergency department with acute gastrointestinal symptoms accompanied by neurological and cardiovascular manifestations following reef fish consumption. Prompt recognition and supportive care can prevent unnecessary investigations, reduce morbidity, and ensure favourable clinical outcomes.

articles.title: Recognizing atypical presentations of idiopathic intracranial hypertension in clinical practice

affiliations.text: Department of Neurology, KIMSHEALTH, Trivandrum, Kerala, India.

abstract.text: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH) usually presents with headache, papilledema, and sixth nerve palsy; however, atypical manifestations may delay diagnosis. Atypical presentations in the present case series were trigeminal neuralgia, focal seizures with Todd's paresis, hypoglossal nerve palsy, intractable migraine-like headache, orthostatic intolerance, and spontaneous cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) rhinorrhea. Most patients showed improvement with medical therapy, with only two requiring surgical intervention. These findings show that atypical manifestations of IIH are not uncommon and that measuring cerebrospinal fluid opening pressure is essential for timely diagnosis.

Introduction

Idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH) is characterized by elevated intracranial pressure (ICP) without an identifiable structural cause. The classic clinical features include headache, papilledema, diplopia due to sixth nerve palsy, transient visual obscurations, and pulsatile tinnitus.1 However, atypical presentations, although recognized in the literature, remain underdiagnosed and may result in prolonged diagnostic delays.

Reported atypical manifestations include IIH without papilledema (IIHWOP), unilateral or highly asymmetric papilledema, trigeminal neuralgia, facial palsy, olfactory dysfunction, auditory and vestibular symptoms, seizures, radiculopathy, and spontaneous skull base CSF leaks.2 Other rare presentations of IIH include pseudo-Foster Kennedy syndrome3 and cyclic vomiting syndrome.4 Such atypical presentations warrant consideration of IIH, particularly in young obese women, even in the absence of the classic signs. There are few case reports of atypical presentation of IIH from India,3,5,6 Saudi Arabia,7,8 USA4 and Germany.9

Case descriptions

Case 1: Trigeminal neuralgia as a manifestation of IIH

A 45-year-old woman presented with a five-year history of chronic right-sided facial pain localized to the maxillary (V2) distribution of the trigeminal nerve. The pain was sharp, episodic, and triggered by touch, consistent with trigeminal neuralgia. Neurological examination was otherwise unremarkable and showed no papilledema. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain with venography revealed a partial empty sella and kinking of the optic nerves. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) opening pressure (OP) was 27 cm H2O, confirming elevated intracranial pressure. A diagnosis of atypical IIH presenting with trigeminal neuralgia was made. The patient responded well to acetazolamide therapy.

Case 2: Focal motor seizures with Todd's paresis

A 48-year-old woman with longstanding hypertension and hypothyroidism presented with recurrent right brachial focal motor seizures, occasionally followed by Todd's paresis. The symptoms had been present for 12 months. Neuroimaging demonstrated a complete empty sella, enlarged optic nerve sheath, and a prominent Meckel's cave, suggestive of chronically elevated intracranial pressure. CSF OP measured 25 cm H2O. There was no papilledema. A diagnosis of IIH presenting atypically with seizures was made. The patient showed improvement on acetazolamide and topiramate therapy.

Case 3: IIH without papilledema (IIHWOP) presenting as chronic headache

A 39-year-old woman with hypothyroidism and vitamin D deficiency presented with a 14-month history of chronic headache. Fundus examination showed no papilledema. MRI of the brain showed partial empty sella, mild tortuosity of both optic nerves, and increased perioptic CSF spaces. CSF OP was 27 cm H2O, supporting the diagnosis of IIHWOP. The patient demonstrated symptomatic improvement with acetazolamide therapy.

Case 4: CSF rhinorrhea revealing underlying IIH

A 40-year-old woman developed clear watery nasal discharge immediately after a nasopharyngeal COVID-19 swab test. Beta-2 transferrin testing confirmed CSF rhinorrhea. Computed tomography (CT) cisternography showed a 1.7-mm skull base defect involving the left posterior cribriform plate. MRI revealed empty sella, increased perioptic CSF spaces, optic nerve kinking, and bilateral transverse sinus stenosis. CSF OP was markedly elevated at 34 cm H2O. The patient underwent surgical repair of the skull-base defect and was subsequently managed for IIH with acetazolamide.

Case 5: Hypoglossal nerve palsy with dysarthria

A 47-year-old woman with hypertension presented with acute dysarthria and left-sided headache of seven days' duration. Examination revealed left hypoglossal (XII) nerve palsy, with deviation of the tongue to the left on protrusion and to the right at rest, consistent with lower motor neuron involvement. MRI of the brain showed complete empty sella and optic nerve sheath enlargement. CSF OP was 28 cm H2O. This rare example of IIH presenting with isolated hypoglossal palsy responded to acetazolamide and blood pressure control.

Case 6: Orthostatic intolerance associated with IIH

A 24-year-old woman with hypothyroidism presented with a two-month history of intermittent brief episodes of giddiness on standing. She denied significant headache or visual symptoms. MRI revealed complete empty sella and optic nerve sheath distension. Her CSF OP was markedly elevated at 39 cm H2O. Despite the absence of headache, imaging and CSF findings supported the diagnosis of IIH. The patient showed improvement with acetazolamide therapy, along with advice on volume status and postural precautions.

Case 7: IIH without papilledema presenting with migraine-like headache

A 19-year-old morbidly obese woman presented with a two-year history of migraine-like headaches without aura. She had no papilledema. MRI demonstrated complete empty sella and optic nerve sheath enlargement. CSF OP was 44 cm H2O, confirming significantly raised intracranial pressure. She was diagnosed with IIHWOP and treated with acetazolamide along with a structured weight-reduction therapy. Because the headache remained refractory, a lumbo-peritoneal (LP) shunt was inserted to relieve intracranial pressure.

Treatment and outcomes

Five patients were treated with acetazolamide. Two patients received a combination of acetazolamide and topiramate. Case 4 required trans-nasal surgical repair of a skull base defect and Case 7 required LP shunt placement. Most patients experienced clinical improvement. No recurrences were noted during the available follow-up period.

Discussion

In this cohort, seven of 54 patients (12.9%) with IIH exhibited atypical features, consistent with previous reports indicating that atypical presentations constitute a substantial minority of IIH patients. A striking finding was that all affected individuals were women, reaffirming the well-established female predominance in IIH.11 The spectrum of atypical manifestations in this study is in agreement with existing literature, and included trigeminal neuropathy, lower cranial nerve involvement, seizure disorders, and spontaneous CSF leaks. Hypoglossal palsy, as observed in Case 5, is particularly rare and highlights the potential of IIH to affect even lower cranial nerves. Similarly, the enlargement of Meckel's cave in the patient presenting with focal seizures echoes previous observations linking chronically elevated ICP with bony remodeling.6

Idiopathic intracranial hypertension without papilledema (IIHWOP) poses a considerable diagnostic challenge. In such cases, characteristic neuroimaging findings and elevated CSF opening pressure assume greater diagnostic importance. Importantly, delayed diagnosis was common in this series, with symptom duration extending to five years in one patient. Early recognition of atypical manifestations may prevent prolonged morbidity and unnecessary diagnostic procedures.

The strong association between obesity and IIH was evident in our study. Weight reduction remains an effective and cost-efficient disease-modifying strategy. Interestingly, previous studies have suggested that Indian patients with typical IIH are not uniformly obese.11 In contrast, obesity was a prominent association among patients with atypical manifestations in the present series. To the best of our knowledge, this represents one of the largest case series describing atypical presentations of IIH.

Conclusion

Atypical IIH can mimic a variety of neurological disorders. Clinicians should maintain a high index of suspicion for IIH in women, particularly those with obesity, presenting with unexplained cranial neuropathies, trigeminal neuralgia, CSF rhinorrhea, or refractory headache even in the absence of papilledema. Early lumbar puncture with measurement of CSF opening pressure is crucial for establishing the diagnosis and avoiding unnecessary investigations. Weight reduction and medical therapy remain effective in most cases.

abstract.heading: Background
abstract.text: Eosinophilic meningitis (EM) is a rare pediatric condition characterized by ≥10 eosinophils/mm^3^ or >10% of total cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) leukocytes. The most common cause worldwide is infection with the nematode *Angiostrongylus cantonensis*.

abstract.heading: Methods
abstract.text: We describe three pediatric cases of eosinophilic meningitis admitted to a tertiary care center in Trivandrum, Kerala.

abstract.heading: Results
abstract.text: All patients presented with prolonged fever and meningitis unresponsive to conventional antibiotic therapy. Key laboratory findings included marked peripheral eosinophilia and CSF eosinophilia. All patients had a history of environmental exposure to snails. The diagnosis was confirmed by positive CSF quantitative polymerase chain reaction (qPCR) for *A. cantonensis*. Neuroimaging findings were varied, from normal to punctate ischemia. Treatment with a 14-day course of albendazole combined with corticosteroids led to complete clinical recovery in all cases.

abstract.heading: Conclusion
abstract.text: Pediatric eosinophilic meningitis remains a diagnostic challenge, and requires a high index of clinical suspicion, particularly in regions such as Kerala where exposure to intermediate hosts such as snails is common. Clinicians should consider this diagnosis in children presenting with prolonged fever and features of subacute meningitis that fail to respond to conventional antibiotic therapy. Our case series highlights three important diagnostic considerations: (1) the need for serial monitoring of peripheral absolute eosinophil counts, as initial counts may be normal; (2) the importance of direct communication with the pathologist to specifically screen for eosinophils in CSF smears, which may otherwise be overlooked in routine automated counts; (3) elicitation of environmental exposure history, particularly contact with snails or slugs.

articles.bodyHtml:
Introduction

Eosinophilic meningitis is defined by the presence of ≥10 eosinophils/mm3 in the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) or eosinophils accounting for ≥10% of total CSF leukocytes.1 The condition is rare in India, with only a limited number of pediatric cases reported in the literature.2 The most common cause worldwide is central nervous system (CNS) infection with helminthic parasites, particularly Angiostrongylus cantonensis.3

A. cantonensis has a complex life cycle in which rats serve as definitive hosts and molluscs, including snails and slugs, act as intermediate hosts. Humans acquire the infection accidentally by ingesting raw or undercooked snails, contaminated vegetables, or paratenic (transport) hosts such as freshwater prawns and crabs.4 Following ingestion, larvae crossing the intestinal mucosa may reach the CNS, where they cause mechanical damage (tissue injury) or immune-mediated inflammatory responses. Humans are dead-end hosts, and the parasite is unable to complete its life cycle within the human body.

Other parasites causing eosinophilic meningitis include Gnathostoma spinigerum, Baylisascaris procyonis, and Ascaris lumbricoides. Less commonly, eosinophilic meningitis may be caused by viral, bacterial, or fungal infections, notably coccidioidomycosis. In non-endemic regions, the differential diagnosis includes hypereosinophilic syndrome, malignancy, drug reactions, and sarcoidosis.

Clinical manifestations typically develop 1–3 weeks after exposure and may include prolonged fever, headache, irritability, bulging fontanelle, meningeal signs, cranial nerve palsy, and ataxia. The diagnosis is supported by investigations including that for peripheral eosinophilia, CSF eosinophilia, and molecular detection of A. cantonensis by polymerase chain reaction (PCR). Serological testing may be helpful but is limited by cross-reactivity with other helminthic infections.10

The optimal treatment strategy remains under debate: corticosteroids alone, albendazole monotherapy, or combination regimens have all been used, though concerns exist about anthelmintic-induced inflammation. However, most reported outcomes are favorable.11 Treatment duration is typically two weeks.12

Pediatric eosinophilic meningitis poses a significant diagnostic challenge because its clinical presentation frequently overlaps with that of bacterial or viral meningitis, often resulting in delayed recognition and appropriate therapy.13

We report three pediatric cases of A. cantonensis eosinophilic meningitis from Kerala, highlighting key clinical features, diagnostic challenges, and important lessons for early recognition.

Cases description

Discussion

In our series, three children (two boys and one girl) from different geographic regions presented to a tertiary care hospital in Trivandrum with prolonged fever and neurological symptoms. Two children were below two years of age, consistent with prior pediatric reports.14 All had a history of exposure to snails, reinforcing the epidemiological association with Angiostrongylus cantonensis infection.1

Neurological features included irritability, poor feeding, bulging anterior fontanelle in infants, and unilateral lateral rectus palsy in two children. Neurological symptoms developed approximately one week after the onset of fever.

Peripheral blood eosinophilia was pivotal in guiding further evaluation; however, in two children, initial blood and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) investigations were inconclusive, leading to an initial diagnosis of bacterial meningitis. Persistent fever and neurological symptoms prompted repeat investigations, which demonstrated rising peripheral eosinophils and >10% CSF eosinophils, fulfilling the diagnostic criteria for eosinophilic meningitis.1

MRI findings included punctate diffusion restriction and nonspecific T2 hyperintensities, with one child showing a normal MRI. Similar radiological findings have been described previously in literature.1 All children recovered without neurological sequelae following treatment with a standard regimen of albendazole and oral corticosteroids, consistent with favorable outcomes reported in pediatric eosinophilic meningitis.1 At the last follow-up, all children were asymptomatic, underscoring the importance of clinical vigilance, repeating investigations when initial findings are inconclusive, and instituting timely therapy in endemic regions.

Conclusion

Pediatric eosinophilic meningitis remains a diagnostic challenge in endemic regions such as Kerala, where exposure to intermediate hosts, particularly snails, is common. Clinicians should consider this diagnosis in children presenting with subacute meningitis that is unresponsive to antibiotics. Our series emphasizes three diagnostic pillars: the importance of serial eosinophil counts, as initial peripheral blood and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) eosinophilia may be absent or overlooked; the need for direct communication with pathologists to ensure careful examination of CSF smears for eosinophils; and the value of maintaining a high index of suspicion by integrating epidemiological exposures, evolving laboratory findings, and interdisciplinary dialogue to enable timely recognition and management.

abstract.heading: Introduction
abstract.text: Coagulation factor deficiencies are rare disorders that may first become apparent during pregnancy and are associated with an increased risk of hemorrhage in the antepartum, intrapartum, and postpartum periods. Although pregnancy induces a physiological hypercoagulable state, women with inherited or acquired coagulation factor deficiencies remain susceptible to bleeding complications. Early diagnosis and multidisciplinary management are essential to optimize maternal and neonatal outcomes.

abstract.heading: Case reports
abstract.text: We report two cases of previously undiagnosed coagulation factor deficiencies identified during pregnancy. The first case involved a 24-year-old woman with recurrent antepartum bleeding and progressive subchorionic hemorrhage beginning in early pregnancy. Routine coagulation studies were normal, but factor assay revealed severe factor XIII deficiency. She was successfully managed with weekly cryoprecipitate transfusions and tranexamic acid, resulting in a term delivery without excessive bleeding. The second case involved a 35-year-old woman who was found to have an isolated prolongation of activated partial thromboplastin time during routine antenatal evaluation. Further investigations demonstrated severe factor XI deficiency, which was subsequently confirmed by genetic testing. Following prophylactic fresh frozen plasma transfusion, she underwent an uncomplicated vaginal delivery and had an uneventful postpartum course.

abstract.heading: Discussion
abstract.text: These cases highlight the diverse clinical presentations of coagulation factor deficiencies in pregnancy and the limitations of routine coagulation screening. Accurate diagnosis requires a high index of suspicion and the use of targeted coagulation factor assays. Management should be individualized and involve close collaboration among maternal fetal medicine specialists, obstetricians, hematologists, anesthesiologists, and neonatologists.

abstract.heading: Conclusion
abstract.text: Timely recognition and multidisciplinary management of coagulation factor deficiencies can result in favorable maternal and neonatal outcomes, even in women whose disorders first become apparent during pregnancy.
