articles.bodyHtml:
Introduction

Bleeding disorders include coagulation factor deficiencies (both congenital and acquired), platelet disorders, fibrinolytic defects, and vascular disorders. These conditions may manifest as spontaneous or provoked bleeding or may remain asymptomatic. Normal pregnancy is characterized by a procoagulant state. Important changes include increased levels of factors VII, VIII, X, XII, and fibrinogen; decreased levels of factors XI and XIII; increased von Willebrand factor (vWF); reduced protein S activity; and reduced fibrinolytic activity due to increased plasminogen activator inhibitors. These physiological adaptations prepare the body for delivery and placental separation. In women with coagulation factor deficiencies, however, this hemostatic balance is disturbed, and the risk of hemorrhage may persist throughout pregnancy, delivery, and the postpartum period.1

Von Willebrand disease (vWD) is the most common inherited disorder of hemostasis and results from quantitative (types 1 and 3) or qualitative (type 2) defects of von Willebrand factor (VWF). Depending on the vWD subtype, inheritance may be autosomal dominant or recessive. Physiological increases in VWF and factor VIII levels during pregnancy may normalize these levels, particularly in women with type 1 and some forms of type 2 disease. Following delivery, these levels decline rapidly, increasing the risk of postpartum hemorrhage and the need for blood product transfusion. Management during childbirth and the postpartum period includes desmopressin or replacement therapy with VWF-containing factor VIII concentrates.2

Hemophilia is inherited in an X-linked recessive manner and primarily affects males, while females are usually carriers, although some may be affected. During pregnancy, factor VIII levels may increase in hemophilia A carriers, whereas factor IX levels in hemophilia B carriers generally remain unchanged. Consequently, these women remain at risk of antepartum, intrapartum, and postpartum hemorrhage. Assessment of factor levels during the third trimester, careful delivery planning, avoidance of traumatic obstetric procedures whenever possible, and appropriate factor replacement therapy are essential to optimize maternal and neonatal outcomes.

Factor XI deficiency is particularly prevalent among individuals of Ashkenazi Jewish ancestry, although it occurs in all populations. Unlike hemophilia, the severity of bleeding correlates poorly with plasma factor levels, and clinical manifestations vary considerably among affected individuals. Factor XI levels generally remain stable during pregnancy and do not exhibit the physiological increase observed with some other coagulation factors. Consequently, affected women remain at risk of bleeding complications throughout pregnancy and the puerperium. Postpartum hemorrhage is the most important obstetric complication, and excessive bleeding may occur following cesarean section, operative vaginal delivery, or other invasive procedures. Management should be individualized according to the patient's bleeding history, factor XI level, and planned mode of delivery. Women with a significant bleeding history or those undergoing high-risk procedures may require replacement therapy with factor XI concentrate, where available, or fresh frozen plasma (FFP). Antifibrinolytic agents such as tranexamic acid are useful adjuncts and are commonly administered during the postpartum period to reduce the risk of secondary postpartum hemorrhage.3

Deficiencies of factors I, II, V, VII, X, XIII, and other rare coagulation factors may result in significant obstetric complications, including recurrent miscarriage, placental abruption, and severe postpartum hemorrhage. Factor XIII deficiency is particularly associated with recurrent pregnancy loss because of its essential role in placental implantation and maintenance.4 Management depends on the specific deficiency and generally involves replacement therapy with factor concentrates, fresh frozen plasma, or cryoprecipitate.

Because coagulation factor deficiency disorders are uncommon, many clinicians encounter them infrequently. Awareness of their clinical manifestations and management is essential for ensuring safe obstetric care. Here, we report two cases of rare coagulation factor deficiencies with distinct clinical presentations that were recognized for the first time during pregnancy.

Case reports

Case 1

A 24-year-old second gravida, with no personal or family history of bleeding diathesis and a previous uneventful pregnancy resulting in a term cesarean section, presented with multiple episodes of vaginal bleeding since 10 weeks of gestation. The bleeding was unresponsive to progesterone therapy, and serial ultrasonographic examinations demonstrated progressively increasing subchorionic hemorrhage. Investigations revealed moderate anemia with a normal platelet count, normal conventional coagulation profile, and normal platelet aggregation studies. Factor assay demonstrated severe factor XIII deficiency (<4%). Inhibitor assay was negative, confirming severe inherited factor XIII deficiency.

She was managed with weekly cryoprecipitate transfusions to maintain factor XIII levels above 15% and tranexamic acid for acute bleeding episodes. She subsequently underwent an elective cesarean section at term without excessive intrapartum or postpartum bleeding.

Case 2

A 35-year-old second gravida, with no personal or family history of bleeding diathesis and a previous uncomplicated vaginal delivery, was found to have an isolated prolonged activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT; 63 seconds) during routine pre-delivery laboratory evaluation. The prolonged aPTT corrected on mixing studies. Factor XI assay demonstrated severe deficiency (<10%). Next-generation sequencing identified a pathogenic variant in the F11 gene.

She received prophylactic fresh frozen plasma (FFP) transfusion before induction of labor and subsequently had an uncomplicated vaginal delivery. The postpartum period was uneventful.

Discussion

These two cases illustrate how rare coagulation factor deficiencies in pregnancy may remain clinically silent until revealed either by obstetric complications or by abnormal antenatal investigations. They also demonstrate two distinct diagnostic pathways. In both women, there was no personal or family history suggestive of a bleeding disorder, and both had previously uncomplicated pregnancies, which could easily have lowered clinical suspicion. However, the current pregnancies revealed subtle but important clues that prompted further evaluation and ultimately led to the diagnosis of rare inherited factor deficiencies.

The first case highlights the importance of considering factor XIII deficiency in women with recurrent antenatal bleeding despite normal conventional coagulation tests. As factor XIII acts after fibrin formation to stabilize the fibrin clot, its deficiency is not detected by routine coagulation screening and requires a specific factor XIII assay for diagnosis.5

In this case, persistent bleeding with progressive subchorionic hematoma despite otherwise unremarkable laboratory findings was the key clue. Severe factor XIII deficiency is classically associated with recurrent early pregnancy loss due to defective placental implantation and maintenance. However, our patient had a different phenotype, presenting with persistent antenatal bleeding and an ongoing viable pregnancy rather than recurrent miscarriage. Recognition of this atypical presentation enabled timely replacement therapy with cryoprecipitate and continuation of pregnancy to term. This case underscores an important lesson for obstetricians: normal PT and aPTT values do not exclude an inherited bleeding disorder, and factor XIII deficiency should be considered in women with unexplained recurrent early pregnancy bleeding or pregnancy loss.

In a retrospective French cohort, Rugeri et al.6 evaluated 11 women with severe factor XIII deficiency and reported that most pregnancies managed with factor XIII replacement had favorable obstetric outcomes without major hemorrhagic complications, although miscarriage remained common. Similarly, Thangaraj et al.7 described factor XIII deficiency in a mother–infant dyad, highlighting its association with recurrent pregnancy loss and neonatal bleeding, including intracranial hemorrhage. Together, these reports reinforce the association between factor XIII deficiency and adverse pregnancy outcomes while emphasizing that timely diagnosis and prophylactic replacement therapy can significantly improve maternal and fetal outcomes. Our case adds to this literature by demonstrating that severe factor XIII deficiency may also present as persistent subchorionic hemorrhage in an ongoing viable pregnancy, even in the absence of prior miscarriage or a prior bleeding history.

The second case represents a contrasting scenario in which the diagnosis arose not from bleeding symptoms but from an isolated prolonged activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) detected during routine pre-delivery investigations. The prolonged aPTT corrected on mixing studies, indicating a factor deficiency rather than the presence of an inhibitor, and subsequent assay confirmed severe factor XI deficiency. This sequence is clinically important because isolated prolongation of aPTT in pregnancy may be overlooked, especially in women without a bleeding history, or attributed to laboratory artifacts. In this patient, the abnormal aPTT was appropriately followed by a mixing study, which proved to be the pivotal diagnostic step. This case demonstrates that an isolated prolonged aPTT may be the first clue to an intrinsic pathway factor deficiency such as factor XI deficiency. It also emphasizes that previous uncomplicated pregnancies do not exclude an inherited coagulation disorder, particularly in factor XI deficiency, where the bleeding phenotype is variable and correlates poorly with factor levels.

Newman et al.,8 in a cohort of 58 women with factor XI deficiency, reported a postpartum hemorrhage rate of 16%. They also found that prophylactic interventions such as tranexamic acid or fresh frozen plasma did not significantly reduce postpartum hemorrhage or transfusion requirements and that factor XI levels at admission correlated poorly with blood loss. Correia et al.9 studied 45 pregnancies in women with factor XI deficiency and observed that factor XI levels remained relatively stable throughout pregnancy. Although some women received prophylactic treatment based on low factor levels, prolonged aPTT, or anticipated neuraxial anesthesia, no patient experienced bleeding complications during pregnancy or delivery. These studies illustrate the variable bleeding phenotype in factor XI deficiency and support individualized management based on bleeding history, factor level, and anticipated obstetric interventions rather than laboratory values alone.

These cases highlight the heterogeneity of presentation of rare coagulation factor deficiencies in pregnancy. In the first case, diagnosis required a high index of suspicion despite normal screening tests because the clinical findings were discordant with the laboratory profile. In the second case, diagnosis depended on careful interpretation of an abnormal screening test in an otherwise asymptomatic woman.

Management in both pregnancies was guided by the underlying pathophysiology of the specific deficiency and the anticipated hemostatic challenges of pregnancy and delivery. In the woman with severe factor XIII deficiency, the principal aim was maintenance of pregnancy and prevention of placental bleeding through sustained replacement therapy. In contrast, the woman with factor XI deficiency remained asymptomatic antenatally and required prophylaxis mainly around delivery, when tissue trauma and postpartum uterine involution increase the risk of bleeding.

These cases offer several practical lessons for obstetricians. A previous uncomplicated pregnancy does not exclude an inherited coagulation disorder. Persistent antenatal bleeding with normal routine coagulation studies should prompt further evaluation. Conversely, an isolated prolonged aPTT should always be investigated systematically. Early involvement of maternal-fetal medicine specialists, obstetricians, hematologists, anesthesiologists, and transfusion services is essential for individualized antenatal, intrapartum, and postpartum planning.10

In summary, careful interpretation of clinical and laboratory findings, timely use of specific factor assays, and multidisciplinary planning can transform potentially high-risk pregnancies into successful maternal and neonatal outcomes.

Conclusion

Coagulation factor deficiencies in pregnancy are rare but clinically significant. With careful assessment, regular monitoring, and coordinated multidisciplinary care, most women can achieve safe pregnancies and deliveries. Individualized management is essential because bleeding risk varies widely between disorders and among affected women. Assessment of factor levels during the third trimester, careful planning of delivery, avoidance of traumatic obstetric procedures when possible, and appropriate factor replacement therapy are essential to optimize maternal and neonatal outcomes.

abstract.text: Prolonged fever with non-specific systemic manifestations poses a significant diagnostic challenge, particularly when caused by uncommon infections. We report a case of a 41-year-old man who presented with prolonged fever and was initially treated for presumed enteric fever. He was subsequently readmitted with recurrent fever and worsening low back pain, and magnetic resonance imaging revealed L5 spondylodiscitis with prevertebral abscess formation. Conventional microbiological investigations and serological testing were inconclusive, whereas whole-genome shotgun metagenomic sequencing of aspirated abscess material identified *Brucella melitensis* as the causative organism. The patient responded favorably to combination antimicrobial therapy, with both clinical and radiological improvement. This case underscores the importance of considering spinal involvement in patients with recurrent fever and back pain and demonstrates the utility of metagenomic sequencing in establishing the diagnosis of culture-negative focal infections.

articles.bodyHtml:
Introduction

Brucellosis is a globally prevalent zoonotic infection caused by intracellular Gram-negative coccobacilli of the genus Brucella. Human infection commonly occurs through consumption of unpasteurized dairy products or occupational exposure to infected animals. The disease is characterized by protean clinical manifestations and often presents as pyrexia of unknown origin.

Musculoskeletal involvement occurs in up to 40% of patients, with spondylodiscitis being among the most severe focal complications. We report a case of Brucella melitensis spondylodiscitis that initially mimicked enteric fever, highlighting the diagnostic challenges posed by this uncommon presentation.

Case presentation

A 41-year-old man with type 2 diabetes mellitus, working in the Middle East, presented with a two-week history of high-grade intermittent fever associated with chills and rigors. The fever had an abrupt onset and persisted despite antipyretic therapy. He also reported cough and generalized fatigue at symptom onset. He also had a history of recent exposure to a roommate with febrile respiratory illness. He frequently consumed food from outside sources and regularly drank long-life packaged milk.

On examination, he was hemodynamically stable. Systemic examination was unremarkable. Initial laboratory investigations revealed a normal total leukocyte count with relative neutrophilia, eosinopenia, and thrombocytopenia. Urinalysis demonstrated glycosuria. Liver function tests showed elevated transaminases. Renal function and serum electrolytes were within normal limits. Inflammatory markers, including C-reactive protein, were elevated. Serum ferritin, triglycerides, and lactate dehydrogenase levels were markedly elevated. Erythrocyte sedimentation rate was within normal limits. Peripheral blood smear did not demonstrate findings suggestive of hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis. Ultrasonography of the abdomen demonstrated mild hepatosplenomegaly. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed preserved ventricular function without evidence of infective endocarditis.

In view of the prolonged fever, thrombocytopenia, transaminitis, and hepatosplenomegaly, enteric fever was initially suspected. Empirical treatment with intravenous ceftriaxone and oral azithromycin was commenced because of the presumed Salmonella-like presentation. Subsequently, the patient developed bicytopenia and a diagnosis of secondary HLH was considered.

Extensive investigations for tropical infections, including malaria, dengue fever, leptospirosis, cytomegalovirus infection, and Epstein–Barr virus infection, were negative. Blood cultures remained sterile. Brucella IgM was positive; however, the result was considered inconclusive because of the possibility of false positivity and a negative agglutination result. The patient was discharged after a week as he demonstrated clinical improvement with no further episodes of fever and improving laboratory parameters.

However, two weeks later, he was readmitted with recurrent high-grade fever and persistent low back pain that had been present since the initial presentation, but had not been considered significant by the patient and was therefore not reported during the initial admission. Following discharge, the low back ache increased markedly in intensity. Clinical examination revealed tenderness in the lower back (L4–L5 region) with restriction of movements. Fever episodes were predominantly nocturnal. Laboratory investigations revealed normal leukocyte counts, normal liver function tests, declining ferritin levels, and mildly elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (40 mm/hour). Repeat blood cultures remained sterile. Repeat Brucella IgM and agglutination tests were negative. Treatment with ceftriaxone and oral doxycycline was commenced.

In view of persistent back pain and recurrent fever spikes, contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging of the lumbosacral spine was performed. Imaging demonstrated heterogeneous marrow signal abnormalities involving the L5 vertebral body and adjacent intervertebral disc, with contrast enhancement and associated prevertebral and paraspinal inflammatory soft tissue collections, consistent with infective spondylodiscitis with prevertebral abscess formation.

Computed tomography-guided aspiration of the abscess was performed.

Conventional microbiological studies were unrevealing; however, whole genome shotgun metagenomic sequencing of the aspirated specimen identified Brucella melitensis as the causative organism.

The patient was subsequently treated with oral doxycycline and rifampicin, in combination with intravenous gentamicin, according to standard therapy for complicated brucellosis. The patient demonstrated significant clinical improvement, with resolution of fever and progressive reduction in back pain.

A follow-up non-contrast MRI of the lumbosacral spine performed after six weeks of antibiotic therapy showed marked radiological improvement compared with the baseline contrast-enhanced study. The previously demonstrated heterogeneous marrow signal abnormality with enhancement involving the L5 vertebral body and adjacent intervertebral disc, along with prevertebral and paraspinal inflammatory soft tissue and small prevertebral/parapsoas abscesses, had largely resolved. The patient thus achieved clinical and radiological remission of brucellar spondylodiscitis.

Discussion

Despite global control efforts, brucellosis remains endemic in several developing countries and continues to represent an important cause of pyrexia of unknown origin. Osteoarticular involvement is the most common focal complication of brucellosis, occurring in approximately 10–85% of affected individuals, with spondylitis and spondylodiscitis representing the most severe forms.

Brucellar spondylodiscitis predominantly affects the lumbar spine, followed by the thoracic and cervical regions. Lumbar involvement has been reported in nearly 60–70% of spinal cases. The disease often presents insidiously with fever, back pain, malaise, weight loss, and elevated inflammatory markers, leading to frequent delays in diagnosis. In endemic regions, spinal brucellosis is commonly misdiagnosed as tuberculous spondylodiscitis because of overlapping radiological and clinical features.

Our patient initially presented with prolonged fever, thrombocytopenia, transaminitis, hepatosplenomegaly, elevated inflammatory markers, and hyperferritinemia, closely mimicking enteric fever and other tropical infections. Transient clinical improvement following ceftriaxone-based therapy further complicated the diagnostic process.

Similar atypical presentations have been described in previous reports in which brucellosis masqueraded as enteric fever, tuberculosis, connective tissue disease, and haematological disorders. Markedly elevated ferritin, triglycerides, and lactate dehydrogenase levels in our patient suggested a hyperinflammatory response resembling secondary hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH). Although true HLH is uncommon in brucellosis, several reports have documented HLH-like syndromes associated with severe brucellar infection.

An important clue in our patient was the recurrence of fever associated with persistent low back pain. Back pain is considered the cardinal symptom of brucellar spondylodiscitis and may precede radiological abnormalities by weeks to months. MRI remains the imaging modality of choice because of its high sensitivity for detecting vertebral marrow edema, disc involvement, paraspinal inflammation, and epidural or prevertebral abscess formation. In our patient, MRI demonstrated L5 vertebral involvement with adjacent discitis and prevertebral soft tissue abscess, findings characteristic of spinal brucellosis.

Microbiological confirmation of brucellosis may be challenging. Blood cultures may be negative in chronic or partially treated disease, and serological tests may yield variable results depending on disease stage and prior antibiotic exposure. In our patient, initial Brucella IgM positivity with negative agglutination testing was interpreted cautiously because of concerns regarding false positivity, while repeat serological testing subsequently became negative. These findings illustrate the limitations of serological testing in focal brucellosis. Similar diagnostic challenges have been emphasized in previous case reports of brucellar spondylodiscitis.

In our patient, the definitive diagnosis was established using metagenomic shotgun sequencing of aspirated abscess material, which identified Brucella melitensis. This represents a clinically significant aspect of the case because whole genome shotgun metagenomic sequencing has emerged as a powerful diagnostic modality for culture-negative infections.

A 2023 report described a case of spinal infection due to Brucella melitensis diagnosed by metagenomic next-generation sequencing in a non-endemic region, highlighting the utility of molecular diagnostics in atypical presentations.1 Similar to our patient, conventional investigations in that case too were inconclusive prior to molecular identification of the organism.

Literature has shown that in a 72-year-old patient initially suspected to have spinal tuberculosis because of chronic back pain and MRI findings of infective spondylodiscitis, diagnosis was ultimately established through Brucella serology.2 Thoracic brucellar spondylodiscitis initially treated as tuberculous disease before relapse prompted reevaluation and microbiological confirmation of brucellosis in yet another case.3 A complex case involving Brucella melitensis endocarditis and spondylitis in a shepherd with prolonged fever and back pain too has been reported, underscoring the protean manifestations of focal brucellosis.4

Another distinctive feature in the case of our patient was the history of clear epidemiological exposure during the initial presentation. Many previously reported patients had identifiable risk factors such as farming, livestock exposure or consumption of unpasteurized dairy products. The history of exposure to packaged long-life milk in our patient had also contributed to the initial clinical suspicion for brucellosis.

Treatment recommendations for brucellar spondylodiscitis advocate prolonged multidrug antimicrobial therapy. Regimens containing doxycycline, rifampicin, and an aminoglycoside such as gentamicin or streptomycin are commonly employed, particularly in complicated spinal disease. Early diagnosis and targeted therapy are essential to prevent neurological complications, spinal instability, chronic pain, and relapse.

This case highlights several important clinical lessons. First, brucellosis should remain an important differential diagnosis in patients with prolonged fever, hepatosplenomegaly, thrombocytopenia, and elevated inflammatory markers, particularly in endemic settings. Second, persistent or recurrent back pain following apparent resolution of febrile illness warrants prompt evaluation for spinal involvement. Finally, molecular diagnostic techniques such as metagenomic sequencing can significantly improve diagnostic yield in culture-negative focal infections and may facilitate timely institution of definitive therapy.

abstract.heading: Background
abstract.text: Spontaneous tumor lysis syndrome (STLS) is a rare but life-threatening oncologic emergency that occurs in the absence of cytotoxic therapy. It results from rapid tumor cell turnover and lysis, leading to severe metabolic derangements and acute kidney injury (AKI). Early recognition, particularly before the diagnosis of an underlying malignancy, remains challenging.

abstract.heading: Case presentation
abstract.text: A 36-year-old male with no known comorbidities presented with myalgia, vomiting, and low-grade fever. Initial evaluation revealed pancytopenia, elevated serum creatinine (4.3 mg/dL), and hyperuricemia (15.9 mg/dL). Infectious, autoimmune, and hematologic investigations were inconclusive, and bone marrow examination showed trilineage hematopoiesis without evidence of malignancy. Following transient clinical improvement, he was discharged. But subsequently, he presented with generalized lymphadenopathy and leukocytosis with atypical lymphocytes. During evaluation, he developed spontaneous tumor lysis syndrome characterized by severe hyperuricemia (41 mg/dL), hyperphosphatemia (16 mg/dL), hyperkalemia (7.9 mmol/L), and worsening renal dysfunction. Aggressive management with intravenous hydration, rasburicase, febuxostat, electrolyte correction, isotonic bicarbonate infusion, and sustained low-efficiency dialysis (SLED) was initiated. Subsequent flow cytometry and lymph node biopsy confirmed T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma (T-ALL). The patient was started on a modified Berlin–Frankfurt–Münster (BFM) protocol.

abstract.heading: Conclusion
abstract.text: STLS may be the initial manifestation of aggressive hematologic malignancies such as T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma (T-ALL). Early recognition and prompt metabolic management are critical to prevent multiorgan failure and improve outcomes.

articles.bodyHtml:
Introduction

Tumor lysis syndrome (TLS) is an oncologic emergency resulting from rapid lysis of malignant cells, leading to the release of intracellular metabolites into the circulation.1 This causes hyperuricemia, hyperkalemia, hyperphosphatemia, and secondary hypocalcemia, which may precipitate acute kidney injury, cardiac arrhythmias, seizures, and death.2

TLS typically occurs following the initiation of chemotherapy in patients with high-grade hematologic malignancies. However, spontaneous tumor lysis syndrome (STLS), which occurs in the absence of cytotoxic therapy, is rare and diagnostically challenging.3 It has been described in aggressive malignancies, particularly lymphomas and leukemias, including T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (T-ALL).4

Recognition of STLS prior to a definitive cancer diagnosis is difficult but essential, as delayed management can lead to catastrophic outcomes. We report a case of STLS presenting as the initial manifestation of T-ALL, complicated by severe metabolic derangements and acute kidney injury requiring sustained low-efficiency dialysis.

Case presentation

A 36-year-old male with no known comorbidities presented with myalgia, vomiting, and low-grade fever. There was no history of weight loss, bleeding manifestations, or prior malignancy.

Initial evaluation

Laboratory investigations showed:

  • Pancytopenia
  • Serum creatinine: 4.3 mg/dL
  • Serum uric acid: 15.9 mg/dL

Infectious and autoimmune workup was negative. Peripheral smear did not reveal blasts. Bone marrow examination demonstrated trilineage hematopoiesis without evidence of malignancy.

The patient was managed conservatively with intravenous fluids and supportive therapy. Renal parameters improved transiently, and he was discharged.

Clinical progression

The patient subsequently returned with:

  • Generalized lymphadenopathy
  • Leukocytosis with atypical lymphocytes
  • Progressive renal dysfunction

During evaluation, he developed severe metabolic abnormalities characterized by:

  • Serum uric acid: 41 mg/dL
  • Serum phosphate: 16 mg/dL
  • Serum potassium: 7.9 mmol/L

These findings were consistent with the Cairo–Bishop criteria for spontaneous tumor lysis syndrome.1

Management and diagnosis

The patient was managed with:

  • Aggressive intravenous hydration
  • Rasburicase
  • Febuxostat
  • Electrolyte correction
  • Isotonic bicarbonate infusion
  • Sustained low-efficiency dialysis (SLED)

Following stabilization, further evaluation revealed diffuse positivity for CD3 and strong positivity for terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase (TdT) on flow cytometry.

Lymph node biopsy confirmed T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma (T-ALL).

He was initiated on a modified Berlin–Frankfurt–Münster (BFM) chemotherapy protocol, which he tolerated well.

Discussion

TLS results from rapid tumor cell destruction and the release of intracellular contents, particularly nucleic acids which are metabolized into uric acid.1 Hyperuricemia and calcium-phosphate precipitation contribute to renal injury.2

Spontaneous tumor lysis syndrome (STLS) is uncommon and is thought to result from high tumor proliferation and spontaneous cell turnover exceeding the vascular supply, leading to tumor necrosis.3 It is most associated with aggressive hematologic malignancies.4

This case highlights several important clinical insights. Severe hyperuricemia in the presence of acute kidney injury should raise suspicion for an underlying occult malignancy. A normal initial bone marrow examination does not exclude evolving leukemia, and STLS may precede the diagnosis of hematologic malignancy. Early administration of rasburicase is crucial in preventing renal failure and other life-threatening complications.2

Recognition of STLS requires a high index of suspicion, particularly when metabolic abnormalities are disproportionate to clinical presentation.

Conclusion

Spontaneous tumor lysis syndrome can be the initial manifestation of aggressive hematologic malignancies such as T-ALL. Early identification and aggressive metabolic management are essential to prevent life-threatening complications. Clinicians should maintain vigilance when encountering unexplained metabolic derangements, even in the absence of confirmed malignancy.

articles.title: An elusive diagnosis: Congenital right mesocolic hernia associated with intestinal malrotation in a child

abstract.text: Congenital mesocolic hernias are rare internal hernias associated with intestinal malrotation and can present with nonspecific symptoms, making diagnosis challenging. We report the case of a 7-year-old boy who presented with recurrent episodes of severe colicky abdominal pain and constipation without vomiting. He had undergone laparoscopic appendicectomy three months earlier, but his symptoms persisted despite multiple evaluations. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) showed clustering of bowel loops on the right side of the abdomen, while an upper gastrointestinal contrast study demonstrated the duodenojejunal junction to the right of the midline, suggestive of intestinal malrotation. Exploratory laparotomy revealed a rare congenital right mesocolic hernia with almost the entire small bowel entrapped within a peritoneal sac lateral to the cecum and ascending colon. A Ladd's procedure was performed, and the child had an uneventful recovery with complete resolution of symptoms. This case highlights the importance of considering rare internal hernias in children with recurrent unexplained abdominal pain.

articles.bodyHtml:
Introduction

Intestinal malrotation is a congenital abnormality occurring in 0.2%–1% of the population. It results from partial or complete failure of normal rotation of the embryologic midgut and includes the full spectrum of rotational anomalies that arise during midgut development.1,2 Congenital internal hernias represent one such variant. They occur when the colonic mesentery fails to fuse with the parietal peritoneum, leaving a free peritoneal reflection that creates a potential space through which small-bowel loops may herniate. Entrapment within these abnormal peritoneal recesses can lead to strangulation and intestinal ischemia, making any internal hernia potentially life-threatening.3 Because symptoms are often nonspecific, internal hernias are often not correctly diagnosed preoperatively.4 Given the rarity of this condition, we report a case of a congenital mesocolic hernia. Notably, despite the child having undergone a prior laparoscopy, the underlying pathology remained undetected.

Case report

A 7-year-old boy presented to the outpatient department with complaints of intermittent episodes of severe colicky abdominal pain. There was no history of vomiting, although he had a history of constipation. He was not on any regular medications, had no known allergies, and there was no significant family history.

The child had undergone a laparoscopic appendicectomy three months prior to presentation at our center. Physical examination at presentation was unremarkable. He had previously been evaluated at multiple healthcare facilities, but no definitive diagnosis had been established. A contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) scan performed at the referring center demonstrated clustering of bowel loops on the right side of the abdomen, prompting referral to our institution for further evaluation.

A water-soluble contrast study performed at our center revealed the duodenojejunal (DJ) junction to the right of the midline, with the majority of the small bowel loops located on the right side of the abdomen. Free passage of contrast was noted, with no evidence of volvulus (Figure 1).

In view of the persistent symptoms and imaging findings, the child was taken up for exploratory laparotomy. Intraoperatively, malrotation of the midgut associated with a right mesocolic hernia was identified. Nearly the entire small intestine, except for the terminal ileum, was found entrapped within a peritoneal sac located lateral to the cecum and ascending colon, with the neck of the sac situated medially. The duodenojejunal junction was noted to lie to the right of the vertebral column (Figure 2).

A Ladd's procedure was performed. The postoperative course was uneventful, and the child recovered well. On follow-up, he remained asymptomatic with complete resolution of abdominal pain.

Discussion

Congenital mesocolic hernias comprise the right and left mesocolic variants described by Willwerth and colleagues. The term 'mesocolic' is preferred to the alternative term 'paraduodenal'. A right mesocolic hernia results from failure of the prearterial limb of the midgut to rotate around the superior mesenteric artery, leading to entrapment of small bowel loops by the mesentery of the cecum and the ascending colon.2 In contrast, a left mesocolic hernia develops when the unsupported segment of the descending mesocolon (between the inferior mesenteric vein and the posterior parietal colonic attachment) balloons outwards as the small intestine migrates into the left superior portion of the abdominal cavity.5,6 In most cases, the cecum completes its rotation and occupies a normal position in the right lower quadrant, while the ileum exits the hernial sac at a variable distance from the ileocecal valve.2,3

In our patient, the findings were consistent with a right-sided mesocolic hernia. Left mesocolic hernias are more frequently reported. Right mesocolic hernias are rarer and often more challenging to diagnose. The non-specific clinical presentation and the rarity of the condition frequently lead to diagnostic uncertainty and may occasionally be misattributed to functional or psychological causes.6

This case is particularly noteworthy because of the diagnostic difficulty encountered despite prior surgical intervention. The child had undergone laparoscopic appendicectomy at a local hospital three months earlier, yet the underlying congenital anomaly remained unrecognized. This highlights how right mesocolic hernias may be easily overlooked because of their rarity, intermittent nature of symptoms, and absence of acute intestinal obstruction at presentation. The case further underscores that even direct intra-abdominal visualization during previous surgery may fail to identify such anomalies unless they are specifically suspected. Therefore, persistent or recurrent unexplained abdominal pain in children warrants thorough reassessment, and rare congenital internal hernias should remain an important differential diagnosis despite previous normal or inconclusive investigations or surgical exploration.

Conclusion

Mesocolic hernias may present either as an acute surgical emergency or as an incidental finding. Surgeons need to be familiar with the embryological basis of mesocolic hernias and their anatomic variations, because both diagnosis and surgical repair depend heavily on this knowledge. A thorough evaluation should be conducted before symptoms of non-specific abdominal pain are attributed to functional causes. Also, timely surgical intervention is crucial to prevent the morbidity and potential mortality associated with acute presentations of mesocolic hernia and resultant small bowel ischemia.

abstract.heading: Background
abstract.text: Post-transplant secondary erythrocytosis (PTE) is an uncommon but well-recognized complication after renal transplantation, characterized by persistent elevation of hemoglobin and hematocrit in patients with a functioning renal allograft. It typically develops within the first two years post-transplant, although delayed presentations can also occur.

abstract.heading: Case presentation
abstract.text: A 53-year-old male with long-standing type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, coronary artery disease, and diabetic nephropathy progressed to end-stage renal disease requiring maintenance hemodialysis in 2019. He underwent a living unrelated donor renal transplantation on April 13, 2021 and was maintained on tacrolimus, mycophenolate mofetil, and prednisolone. Four years after transplantation, routine follow-up revealed erythrocytosis with hemoglobin of 17 g/dL and hematocrit of 56.5%. Renal allograft function was preserved with serum creatinine of 0.8 mg/dL. Evaluation showed a serum erythropoietin level of 14.3 mIU/mL. JAK2 mutation was not detected. Ultrasonography showed a normal transplant kidney in the right iliac fossa, retained native kidneys, and no splenomegaly. After excluding primary myeloproliferative disorders, a diagnosis of late-onset post-transplant erythrocytosis was established.

abstract.heading: Management and outcome
abstract.text: The patient underwent therapeutic phlebotomy for hematocrit control. A total of ten sessions were performed, with approximately 350 mL of blood removed per session. Following treatment, hemoglobin decreased from 17 g/dL to 13.1 g/dL and hematocrit reduced from 56.5% to 46%.

abstract.heading: Conclusion
abstract.text: This uncommon case highlights a delayed presentation of post-transplant erythrocytosis occurring four years after successful renal transplantation. Excellent graft function and retained native kidneys may contribute to persistent erythropoiesis. Long-term hematological surveillance remains important even in clinically stable transplant patients.

articles.bodyHtml:
Introduction

Kidney transplantation is the preferred treatment for end-stage renal disease and usually corrects the anemia associated with chronic kidney disease. However, a subset of recipients develop post-transplant erythrocytosis (PTE), defined as persistent elevation of hemoglobin (>16.5 g/dL in men and 16 g/dL in women) or hematocrit (>51%) after renal transplantation.1

PTE occurs in approximately 8–15% of renal transplant recipients and usually develops within 8–24 months after transplantation.2 Persistent erythrocytosis can increase blood viscosity and may predispose patients to thromboembolic complications.1

The pathogenesis of PTE is multifactorial. It involves persistent erythroid production by retained native kidneys together with normal erythropoietin production by the transplanted kidney, activation of the renin–angiotensin system, increased androgen activity, and restoration of bone marrow responsiveness following correction of uremia.1,2

We report a case of late-onset post-transplant erythrocytosis occurring four years after living unrelated renal transplantation in a patient with excellent graft function who required repeated therapeutic phlebotomy.

Case presentation

A 53-year-old male with type 2 diabetes mellitus for 18 years, hypertension, coronary artery disease with previous inferior wall myocardial infarction, and diabetic retinopathy developed end-stage renal disease secondary to presumed diabetic nephropathy.

He was initiated on maintenance hemodialysis in October 2019 and underwent living unrelated donor renal transplantation on April 13, 2021. The donor was a 40-year-old female. The postoperative period was uneventful, with immediate graft function.

He was maintained on triple immunosuppressive therapy consisting of:

  • Tacrolimus
  • Mycophenolate mofetil
  • Prednisolone

Four years after transplantation, he was detected to have erythrocytosis.

Investigations revealed:

  • Hemoglobin: 17 g/dL
  • Hematocrit: 56.5%
  • Serum creatinine: 0.8 mg/dL
  • Serum erythropoietin: 14.3 mIU/mL (normal)
  • JAK2 mutation analysis: Negative

Ultrasonography showed a well-functioning transplant kidney in the right iliac fossa, retained native kidneys, and no splenomegaly.

The clinical and laboratory findings supported a diagnosis of late-onset post-transplant erythrocytosis.

Management

The patient was not receiving an angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor or angiotensin receptor blocker at presentation.

Therapeutic phlebotomy was initiated to reduce hematocrit. A total of ten sessions were performed, with approximately 350 mL of blood removed during each session.

Following treatment:

  • Hemoglobin reduced to 13.1 g/dL
  • Hematocrit reduced to 46%

Discussion

Post-transplant erythrocytosis (PTE) is a well-recognized hematological complication following renal transplantation. While chronic kidney disease is commonly associated with anemia, restoration of renal function may occasionally result in excessive erythropoiesis.2

The pathogenesis of PTE is multifactorial. Both retained native kidneys and the transplanted kidney may contribute to persistent erythropoietin secretion, leading to stimulation of erythroid progenitor cells and increased red blood cell production.1 Activation of the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system (RAAS) plays a central role in the development of PTE. Increased angiotensin II activity promotes erythropoiesis by stimulating erythropoietin release and enhancing erythroid progenitor proliferation. Angiotensin II may also influence growth factors such as insulin-like growth factor-1, further supporting erythropoiesis.1,2

Successful transplantation and correction of uremia restore bone marrow responsiveness to erythropoietin by eliminating inhibitory factors present during chronic kidney disease. Increased androgen activity may additionally enhance erythropoietin production and erythroid precursor sensitivity.2

Recognized risk factors for PTE include male sex, excellent graft function, retained native kidneys, and absence of rejection episodes.2 Our patient demonstrated several of these factors, including preserved graft function with a serum creatinine level of 0.8 mg/dL and retained native kidneys.

The erythropoietin level of 14.3 mIU/mL was considered inappropriately normal in the presence of elevated hemoglobin and hematocrit levels, supporting dysregulated erythropoiesis and making primary erythrocytosis less likely.

The main differential diagnosis considered was polycythemia vera. Negative JAK2 mutation testing, absence of splenomegaly, and the clinical background favored secondary erythrocytosis related to renal transplantation. ACE inhibitors and angiotensin receptor blockers are considered first-line therapy due to suppression of the renin–angiotensin pathway.2,3 Therapeutic phlebotomy remains useful for hematocrit reduction in selected patients. Our patient showed a good hematological response following repeated phlebotomy sessions.

This case emphasizes that post-transplant erythrocytosis may occur even years after transplantation, highlighting the need for continued long-term monitoring.

Conclusion

Post-transplant erythrocytosis is an important complication that may occur despite excellent renal graft function. Although it is usually seen early after transplantation, delayed presentations should be recognized. Persistent erythropoietin production from retained native kidneys and transplanted kidney, along with restored bone marrow responsiveness, may contribute to its development. Exclusion of primary hematological disorders is essential, and appropriate management helps prevent complications associated with erythrocytosis.

articles.title: Severe drug-induced myalgias after initiation of bempedoic acid in a statin-intolerant patient

affiliations.text: SRM Medical College Hospital & Research Centre, Chennai and ICMR National Institute of Epidemiology, Chennai, India.

abstract.text: Statin intolerance due to muscle-related symptoms is a common cause of poor adherence to lipid-lowering therapy. Bempedoic acid and ezetimibe are frequently used as second-line alternatives in such patients. Although uncommon, muscle-related adverse events may occur with bempedoic acid. We report the case of a middle-aged man with a history of statin intolerance who developed severe myalgias following initiation of bempedoic acid therapy. Symptoms resolved promptly following drug discontinuation. We propose that despite its rarity, a high index of suspicion may help identify such adverse events, especially in individuals with previously documented statin-related muscle symptoms.

articles.bodyHtml:
Introduction

Statin-associated muscle symptoms (SAMS) are well-described and may include myalgia, muscle tenderness, or, in severe cases, rhabdomyolysis.1 Patients with statin intolerance may need alternative lipid-lowering therapies for primary and secondary prevention of cardiovascular disease. A combination of bempedoic acid and ezetimibe is recommended in such patients. Ezetimibe is not associated with muscle toxicity. However, bempedoic acid has rarely been implicated in muscle-related adverse events.2 We report the case of a middle-aged man with a prior history of SAMS who developed muscle symptoms following initiation of bempedoic acid, highlighting the need for a high index of suspicion, as this uncommon adverse effect may be overlooked as a cause of muscle symptoms.

Case report

A 40-year-old man presented to the outpatient department with an insidious onset of progressively worsening pain in both lower limbs for the past three weeks. He described the pain as dull and aching, mostly involving both thighs, buttocks, and calves. The aches aggravated on standing for a while; however, assuming the supine position did not bring significant relief. There was no radiation of pain, and there was no associated weakness, paresthesia, or numbness. Over the preceding few days, these aches had become disabling enough to prevent him from working out at the gym or even walking.

He was neither diabetic nor hypertensive. Routine blood investigations performed a year earlier had revealed elevated total and LDL cholesterol levels, for which he had been prescribed rosuvastatin 5 mg once daily for primary prevention in view of a family history of coronary artery disease. However, within a few days of starting therapy, he developed muscle aches that were much more severe than those experienced during the present episode. Evaluation at that time revealed elevated creatine kinase (CK) levels, without evidence of rhabdomyolysis. Rosuvastatin was discontinued, and the symptoms resolved promptly, supporting a diagnosis of statin-associated muscle symptoms (SAMS).

On examination during the recent episode, he was found well-built and nourished. General examination and systemic examinations were unremarkable, and there was no muscle tenderness. On further inquiry, he revealed that he had recently been started on bempedoic acid 180 mg and ezetimibe 10 mg once daily following a repeat lipid profile that showed a total cholesterol level of 203 mg/dL and an LDL cholesterol level of 160 mg/dL. Given his previous history of SAMS, the treating physician had prescribed this combination and reassured him that these agents are generally not associated with muscle symptoms. Laboratory investigations, including CK levels, were within normal limits. However, the total cholesterol and LDL cholesterol levels had decreased to 140 mg/dL and 74 mg/dL respectively. Other tests, such as vitamin D and TSH, were within normal limits. After discussion with the patient, the combination lipid-lowering therapy was stopped. Five days after cessation, he reported marked improvement in his symptoms, and by the end of one week, he was completely asymptomatic. He was reassured and advised to repeat the lipid profile after a month to determine the need for and options for further lipid-lowering therapy.

Discussion

Statin-associated muscle symptoms (SAMS) include various manifestations such as muscle aches, soreness, cramps, weakness, and, in extreme cases, rhabdomyolysis.3 With an estimated prevalence of 9%, SAMS is considered a major reason for statin intolerance or non-adherence, leading to increased cardiovascular risk.4 Major risk factors for SAMS include older age, low body mass index, previous statin intolerance, hypothyroidism, vitamin D deficiency, higher doses of statins, strenuous exercise, dehydration, and interactions with certain drugs like fibrates.1

For patients with SAMS, several alternative lipid-lowering approaches have been recommended. These include using lower statin doses, switching to hydrophilic statins such as rosuvastatin or pravastatin, or substituting non-statin agents such as ezetimibe and bempedoic acid.1,5,6 In patients who are unable to tolerate these therapies or fail to achieve target lipid levels, PCSK9 inhibitors such as alirocumab and evolocumab may be considered. However, these agents are injectable and relatively expensive.3,7

This case highlights a rare but clinically significant adverse effect of bempedoic acid in a patient with previously documented SAMS. Bempedoic acid is generally considered safe in statin-intolerant individuals as it is activated predominantly in the liver and has minimal activity in skeletal muscle.6 As a result, muscle-related side effects are considered uncommon. However, our patient developed disabling myalgias within 2-3 weeks of initiation of bempedoic acid–ezetimibe combination therapy, with complete resolution of symptoms following drug withdrawal. This temporal relationship suggests a possible causal association.

An additional noteworthy feature in this case was the patient's normal creatine kinase (CK) level despite marked muscle symptoms. This observation underscores that muscle symptoms potentially related to bempedoic acid may occur despite normal creatine kinase levels and that a drug-related etiology should not be excluded solely on the basis of normal laboratory parameters. The prior history of SAMS may also indicate an underlying susceptibility to muscle-related adverse effects from lipid-lowering therapies.6

With increasing use of bempedoic acid in persons with SAMS, clinicians should remain aware of the possibility of muscle-related adverse effects, particularly in patients with a previous history of SAMS. A high index of suspicion, early recognition, and withdrawal of the drug may prevent unnecessary investigations and improve patient quality of life.

Conclusion

Although bempedoic acid is generally considered a safe and effective alternative in statin-intolerant patients, rare muscle-related adverse effects may occur. This case highlights the importance of maintaining a high index of suspicion for drug-related myalgias, even in the presence of normal creatine kinase levels, particularly in individuals with previously documented statin-associated muscle symptoms. Early recognition and withdrawal of the offending agent may prevent unnecessary investigations and improve patient outcomes.

articles.title: Steroid-modified dermatophytosis presenting as tinea pseudoimbricata

affiliations.text: Department of Dermatology, KIMSHEALTH, Trivandrum, Kerala, India.

abstract.text: The irrational use of over-the-counter topical corticosteroids has significantly altered the clinical presentation of superficial dermatophytosis by suppressing local cell-mediated immunity and masking classic diagnostic features. This localized immunosuppression gives rise to steroid-modified dermatophytosis, including *tinea incognito* and atypical variants such as *tinea pseudoimbricata*. We present a case of a 45-year-old immunocompetent woman with a 3-month history of extensive, intense pruritus and extensive plaques involving the abdomen, bilateral flanks, and axillary regions following the unsupervised use of a potent topical corticosteroid. Cutaneous examination revealed large, well-demarcated, scaly plaques, with characteristic concentric rings in the axillary regions consistent with *tinea pseudoimbricata* morphology. Management consisted of discontinuation of topical corticosteroids and initiation of systemic and steroid-free topical antifungal therapy, along with symptomatic treatment. This case highlights the diagnostic challenges posed by steroid-modified dermatophytosis and underscores the need for greater awareness and stricter regulation of over-the-counter corticosteroid availability.

refs: Zacharopoulou A, Tsiogka A, Tsimpidakis A, Lamia A, Koumaki D, Gregoriou S. Tinea incognito: challenges in diagnosis and management. J Clin Med. 2024;13(11):3267.
Kokandi AA. Tinea incognito. Clin Cosmet Investig Dermatol. 2024;17:993-998.
Verma S, Hay RJ. Topical steroid-induced tinea pseudoimbricata: a striking form of tinea incognito. Int J Dermatol. 2015;54(5):e192-e193.
Holubar K, Male O. Tinea incognita vs. tinea incognito. Acta Dermatovenerol Croat. 2002;10(1):39-40.
articles.correspondingAuthor: Sreeparna Balakrishnan, Department of Dermatology, KIMSHEALTH, Trivandrum, Kerala, India.
articles.bodyHtml:
Background

Superficial dermatophytosis has evolved from a manageable superficial fungal infection into a widespread, recalcitrant epidemic, predominantly fuelled by the unchecked availability and irrational abuse of over-the-counter (OTC) potent topical corticosteroids and fixed-dose combinations. When applied to active dermatophyte infections, these potent anti-inflammatory agents suppress local cell-mediated immunity — the primary defense mechanism against fungal pathogens.1,2 This localized immunosuppression facilitates unchecked fungal proliferation and deeper penetration into the stratum corneum, effectively masking the characteristic inflammatory features and inducing highly atypical clinical presentations, collectively termed tinea incognito.1,2,4 In addition, intermittent application and withdrawal of these agents alter the host-pathogen dynamic, resulting in the development of multiple concentric rings of scaling and erythema, a phenomenon clinically recognized as tinea pseudoimbricata.1,3 Recognition of these steroid-modified morphologies is essential for avoiding diagnostic pitfalls and managing extensive, deep-seated dermatophytosis.1,2

Case presentation

A 45-year-old woman residing in Tamil Nadu presented to our dermatology outpatient department with a 3-month history of intense, unremitting itching and progressive skin rashes involving the abdomen, lower abdominal fold, bilateral flanks, and axillary regions.

The patient reported using an over-the-counter potent topical corticosteroid cream obtained directly from a local pharmacy without a prescription. She described a cyclical pattern of temporary symptomatic remission upon application, followed by a severe, exacerbated recurrence of lesions and itching within days of discontinuing the medication. In addition, she observed a change in the morphology of the lesions. She had no known history of diabetes mellitus or immunodeficiencies.

Examination

Physical examination revealed large, extensive well-demarcated patches and plaques over the abdomen, bilateral flanks, axillary regions, and lower abdominal folds. The lesions showed dry scaly eczematous central areas within the patch with some areas showing healed excoriations.

Characteristic concentric rings were evident within the patches, most prominently in the axillary area, imparting a characteristic tinea pseudoimbricata morphology.

Management

The patient was advised to discontinue all topical corticosteroid preparations, with counselling regarding the possibility of a temporary rebound flare following withdrawal.1,2 Given the extensive involvement of multiple anatomical sites and the steroid-modified nature of the infection, systemic oral antifungal therapy was initiated.1,2 A non-steroidal, pure topical antifungal agent was prescribed to be applied to the lesions to target superficial clearance.1,2 Symptomatic treatment included administration of sedating or non-sedating antihistamines to alleviate severe pruritus, in conjunction with barrier-repairing emollients.1,2

Conclusion

This case highlights tinea incognito, a steroid-modified dermatophytic infection in which the classical clinical features, such as an active, scaly annular border, are masked by the inappropriate use of topical immunosuppressive agents.1,2,4

The widespread over-the-counter (OTC) availability of potent topical corticosteroids (TCS) and fixed-dose combination creams continues to pose a major public health challenge in developing countries.1,2,3

Although these medications provide temporary symptomatic relief from pruritus due to their anti-inflammatory properties, they suppress local cell-mediated immunity.1,2 This permits unhindered dermatophytic proliferation, altering the characteristic morphology and leading to a diagnostic dilemma known as tinea incognito.1,2

Awareness of characteristic steroid-modified presentations, including tinea pseudoimbricata, is essential for early diagnosis, avoidance of unnecessary treatments, and appropriate management of extensive dermatophytosis.

pharma.title: Secondary prevention after coronary artery bypass graft surgery: 2026 American Heart Association update
pharma.summary: The AHA's updated scientific statement stresses lifelong, aggressive secondary prevention after CABG, covering antithrombotic, lipid, β-blocker, antihypertensive and diabetes therapy.
refs: Lawton JS, Bhatt DL, de Lemos JA, Bakaeen FG, Hess CN, Alexander JH, et al. Secondary prevention after coronary artery bypass graft surgery: a scientific statement from the American Heart Association. Circulation. 2026;153. doi:10.1161/CIR.0000000000001434.
pharma.bodyHtml:
The American Heart Association (AHA) has published an updated scientific statement on secondary prevention after coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG). While CABG remains a safe and durable treatment for coronary artery disease (CAD), disease progression can continue after surgery, placing patients at ongoing risk of graft failure and recurrent cardiovascular events. The updated guidance emphasizes the importance of lifelong, aggressive secondary prevention. Key practical considerations as mentioned in the AHA guidelines:

Antithrombotic therapy

  • Low-dose aspirin initiated within six hours of CABG and continued indefinitely improves graft patency and reduces future cardiovascular events; higher doses offer no incremental benefit and increase the risk of gastrointestinal bleeding.
  • In patients undergoing CABG for acute coronary syndrome (ACS), dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT) for one year may reduce mortality and cardiac events.
  • For patients with chronic coronary disease, routine DAPT is not recommended.
  • However, one year of DAPT with aspirin plus clopidogrel or ticagrelor may be considered to reduce graft failure in patients without a high bleeding risk.

Lipid management after CABG

Aggressive lipid management is strongly emphasized, with an ideal low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) target of ≤55 mg/dL (1.4 mmol/L).

  • High-intensity or maximally tolerated statin therapy remains the first-line approach.
  • If LDL-C targets are not achieved, ezetimibe should be added.
  • In patients who remain above target despite combination therapy, PCSK9 inhibitors such as evolocumab are recommended.
  • For patients with triglyceride concentrations between 135 and 500 mg/dL (1.5–5.6 mmol/L), icosapent ethyl (omega-3) may be considered to further reduce cardiovascular risk.

β-blocker therapy after CABG

  • Preoperative: No evidence supports β-blocker administration within 24 hours before elective CABG in β-blocker–naive patients.
  • Perioperative: β-blockers are used to prevent AF in high-risk patients. If already on β-blockers, perioperative continuation is associated with a reduction in AF and lower 30-day mortality and ventricular arrhythmias in those with left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) ≤40%.
  • Long-term: Long-term treatment with cardioselective β-blockers appears to reduce major adverse cardiovascular events (MACEs), although a mortality benefit has not been demonstrated.

Antihypertensive therapy after CABG

  • Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors or angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs) should be prescribed according to standard clinical indications for patients who have a clinical indication other than CABG (including previous myocardial infarction, diabetes mellitus, heart failure, reduced LVEF, and hypertension).
  • In patients receiving radial artery grafts, calcium channel blockers during the first postoperative year may help prevent graft spasm. Dihydropyridine agents such as amlodipine or nifedipine are preferred over non-dihydropyridines such as diltiazem or verapamil.

Diabetes management after CABG

The updated statement highlights the expanding role of glucose-lowering agents that provide cardiovascular and renal protection.

  • Sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 (SGLT2) inhibitors are prioritized in post-CABG patients because of their proven cardiovascular and renal benefits, even when glycemic control is adequate.
  • Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) are recommended in post-CABG patients with diabetes or a body mass index (BMI) >27 kg/m2 without diabetes to reduce major adverse cardiac events (MACEs) regardless of glycated hemoglobin levels.

pharma.title: NICE updates type 2 diabetes management with emphasis on cardiorenal protection
pharma.summary: NICE NG28 (February 2026) moves to comorbidity-based first-line therapy, recommending modified-release metformin plus an SGLT2 inhibitor for most people with type 2 diabetes.
refs: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE). Type 2 diabetes in adults: management (NG28). Updated February 2026. London: NICE; 2026. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng28
Visual summary available at: https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng28/resources/visual-summary-full-version-choosing-medicines-for-firstline-and-further-treatment-pdf-10956472093
pharma.bodyHtml:
In February 2026, the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) updated its guideline on the management of type 2 diabetes in adults (NG28), marking a significant shift from the traditional stepwise escalation of therapy to a more individualized, comorbidity-based approach.

The revised guidance recommends modified-release (MR) metformin and SGLT2 inhibitors as first-line therapy for most patients with type 2 diabetes, highlighting their proven cardiovascular and renal benefits as well as the potential for improved treatment adherence. This update reflects a broader shift towards cardiovascular and renal protection alongside glycemic control.

Key changes

  • Dual therapy first: patients newly diagnosed with diabetes mellitus are recommended modified-release metformin plus an SGLT2 inhibitor, unless contraindicated.
  • Triple therapy for ASCVD: patients with atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease may start metformin + SGLT2 inhibitor + subcutaneous semaglutide.
  • Consider triple first-line therapy (metformin, SGLT2 inhibitor, and a GLP-1 RA/tirzepatide) for people with early-onset type 2 diabetes (onset at <40 years) or obesity.

pharma.title: Updated ACG guidelines redefine treatment strategies for Helicobacter pylori infection
pharma.summary: The ACG guideline favours 14-day optimized bismuth quadruple therapy, adds rifabutin and vonoprazan-based regimens, and reserves clarithromycin for confirmed susceptibility.
refs: Chey WD, Mégraud F, Laine L, et al. ACG Clinical Guideline: Treatment of Helicobacter pylori infection. Am J Gastroenterol. 2024;119:1730-1753.
University of Illinois Chicago Drug Information Group. What are the latest guideline recommendations for the treatment of Helicobacter pylori infection in the U.S.? January 2025.
UpToDate. Vonoprazan: Drug information. Updated 2025.
pharma.bodyHtml:
The American College of Gastroenterology (ACG) published an updated guideline in 2024 on the treatment of Helicobacter pylori infection, marking a substantial shift from the 2017 recommendations. The changes reflect rising rates of antimicrobial resistance, wider availability of antibiotic susceptibility testing, and the emergence of newer therapeutic options, including rifabutin-containing regimens and the potassium-competitive acid blocker (P-CAB) vonoprazan.

Treatment regimens as per ACG guidelines (refer to the table below for more information):

Treatment-naïve patients whose antibiotic susceptibility is unknown

ACG recommends optimized bismuth quadruple therapy (BQT) for 14 days as the preferred regimen. For patients without penicillin allergy, empiric alternatives include:

  • Rifabutin-based triple therapy for 14 days.
  • Vonoprazan-amoxicillin dual therapy for 14 days.

Treatment-experienced patients with persistent H. pylori infection

In patients with persistent H. pylori infection, optimized BQT for 14 days is again the preferred regimen for those who have not previously received BQT and for whom antibiotic susceptibility is unknown, or for those who failed to eradicate the infection with initial PPI-clarithromycin triple therapy.

In patients previously treated with optimized BQT, rifabutin triple therapy is a suitable empiric alternative.

Clarithromycin- or levofloxacin-containing salvage regimens should only be used if antibiotic susceptibility has been confirmed.

For treatment-experienced patients with persistent H. pylori infection confirmed to be clarithromycin-sensitive, PPI- or P-CAB–clarithromycin triple therapy is suggested.

Vonoprazan: a new potassium-competitive acid blocker

Vonoprazan is a potassium-competitive acid blocker (P-CAB) approved for the treatment of erosive and non-erosive gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) and as part of combination regimens for Helicobacter pylori eradication.

Dose

  • 10–20 mg once or twice daily, depending on the indication.

Duration of therapy

  • Erosive GERD: 8 weeks
  • Non-erosive GERD: 4–8 weeks
  • H. pylori eradication regimen: 14 days

Missed dose

Take the missed dose as soon as possible within four hours of the scheduled dose. If more than four hours have elapsed, skip the missed dose and resume the regular dosing schedule.

Administration

May be taken orally without regard to meals.

pharma.title: FDA approves dupilumab as the first treatment for allergic fungal rhinosinusitis
pharma.summary: In February 2026 the FDA approved dupilumab (Dupixent) for allergic fungal rhinosinusitis in patients aged six and older after sinonasal surgery.
refs: U.S. Food and Drug Administration. FDA approves drug for adult and pediatric patients aged 6 years and older with allergic fungal rhinosinusitis. February 2026.
Lexicomp Online. Dupilumab: Drug information. Wolters Kluwer Health. Accessed 2026.
pharma.bodyHtml:
In February 2026, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved dupilumab (Dupixent®) for the treatment of allergic fungal rhinosinusitis (AFRS) in adults and children aged six years and older who have previously undergone sinonasal surgery. This approval makes dupilumab the first FDA-approved therapy specifically indicated for AFRS.

Allergic fungal rhinosinusitis is a rare but potentially destructive subtype of chronic rhinosinusitis characterized by an exaggerated immune response to fungal antigens within the sinuses. Patients frequently present with recurrent nasal polyps, chronic nasal obstruction, and allergic mucin accumulation. Progressive disease can lead to bone erosion, orbital involvement, visual impairment, and recurrent need for surgical intervention.

Evidence supporting approval

The FDA approval was based on a 52-week clinical study demonstrating significant improvements in multiple disease parameters among patients receiving dupilumab.

Based on the study findings and the well-established safety profile of dupilumab across several type 2 inflammatory diseases, the FDA concluded that the benefits of treatment outweigh the associated risks in patients with AFRS.

Dupilumab (Dupixent®)

Pharmacologic class

  • Interleukin-4 receptor antagonist
  • Human monoclonal antibody

Mechanism of action

Blocks IL-4 and IL-13 signaling pathways involved in type 2 inflammation.

Route of administration

  • Subcutaneous injection

Dose in allergic fungal rhinosinusitis

  • 300 mg subcutaneously every other week

Approved age group

  • Adults and children aged ≥6 years who have undergone sinonasal surgery

Potential benefits

  • Reduces nasal polyps and congestion
  • Improves sense of smell
  • Decreases corticosteroid requirements
  • Reduces need for repeat surgery
  • May limit sinus bone erosion

spotters.question: Which of the following examination findings helps distinguish a plantar wart from a corn or callus?

B. Tiny, pinpoint black dots visible on the surface

spotters.findings: Plantar warts contain highly vascularized dermal papillae. As the lesion enlarges, or when the overlying thickened skin is pared down, thrombosis of the dilated capillaries produces the characteristic pinpoint black dots, a distinguishing feature that helps differentiate plantar warts from corns and calluses.
